supplier_excerpts.quote:
A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix a separable real Hilbert space $H$ and an integer $k\ge1$. The rule in [[alg-geometric-median-of-block-means]] defines a single-valued Borel map $H^k\to H$: for every tuple $(m_1,\ldots,m_k)$ the function $F_m(z)=\sum_{j=1}^k\|z-m_j\|$ has a nonempty closed convex minimizer set, and that set has a unique point of minimum norm. The choice-free Borel construction below does not use weak compactness or reflexivity. Countable Choice is used only for the published Hilbert projection supplier that identifies the minimum-norm point.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

citations.quote:
Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, let $n\ge1$, and let $1\le k\le n$ be an integer. Given $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in H^n$, put $q=\lfloor n/k\rfloor$ and $r=n-kq$. Form consecutive blocks $B_1,\ldots,B_k$ in index order, with $|B_j|=q+1$ for $j\le r$ and $|B_j|=q$ for $j>r$. Compute the block means $m_j=|B_j|^{-1}\sum_{i\in B_j}x_i$. Return the unique minimum-norm point of
$$
\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in H}\sum_{j=1}^k\|z-m_j\|.
$$

The objective minimizers are called geometric medians of the block means. The minimum-norm rule makes the output single-valued. Existence, uniqueness of that selected point, and Borel measurability as a function of the input tuple are proved in [[lem-measurable-minimum-norm-geometric-median-selection]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $C\subseteq H$ be nonempty, closed and convex, and let $x\in H$. Then there is exactly one point $p\in C$ with $\|x-p\|=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|$, that is, a unique nearest point of $C$ to $x$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with closed sets as in
[[def-metric-topology]] and the finite intersection property as in
[[def-finite-intersection-property]]. For a family $\mathcal{A}$ of subsets of
$X$ write

$$\bigcap \mathcal{A} \;:=\; \{\, x \in X : x \in F \text{ for every } F \in \mathcal{A} \,\},$$

so that $\bigcap \emptyset = X$, matching the convention for the empty finite
intersection in [[def-finite-intersection-property]].

Then $(X,d)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]) **if and only if** every
family $\mathcal{A}$ of closed subsets of $X$ with the finite intersection
property satisfies $\bigcap \mathcal{A} \ne \emptyset$.

No choice principle is used in either direction: complementation is a canonical
bijection, so no member of a family ever has to be selected.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

Let $A$ be a nonempty set. Then $A$ is at most countable ([[def-countable]]) if
and only if there is a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to A$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

Moreover, from any such surjection an injection $A \to \mathbb{N}$ is obtained
explicitly, without any choice, by

$$j(a) := \min\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : s(k) = a \,\}.$$

This is the working form of countability used everywhere below: to prove a
nonempty set countable it suffices to list its elements, repetitions and all.

**No choice principle is used.** The backward direction is where an appeal to
choice would be natural ("for each $a$ pick some $k$ with $s(k) = a$") and it is
avoided outright, because $\min$ is canonical: every nonempty set of naturals has
a *least* element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]), so $j(a)$ is determined by
$a$ and $s$ alone.

derivations.claim: Let $V=\operatorname{span}\{m_1,\ldots,m_k\}$. In the given center order, Gram–Schmidt replaces $m_j$ by $r_j=m_j-\sum_{\ell<j}\langle m_j,e_\ell\rangle e_\ell$ using the previously retained orthonormal vectors; if $r_j=0$ it is skipped, and otherwise $e=r_j/\|r_j\|$ is appended. Induction on the finite list shows the retained vectors are orthonormal and span $V$. For $d=\dim V>0$, if $v_n=\sum_{\ell=1}^d a_{n\ell}e_\ell\in V$ converges in $H$ to $v$, then [F4] gives $a_{n\ell}=\langle v_n,e_\ell\rangle\to\langle v,e_\ell\rangle$ for each $\ell$; the finite sums converge to $\sum_\ell\langle v,e_\ell\rangle e_\ell=v$, so $V$ is closed. If $d=0$, all centers are zero and $F_m(z)=k\|z\|$ has the unique minimizer $0$. For $d>0$, set $P_Vz=\sum_\ell\langle z,e_\ell\rangle e_\ell$; its residual is orthogonal to $V$. Pythagoras gives $\|z-m_j\|^2=\|P_Vz-m_j\|^2+\|z-P_Vz\|^2$, so $F_m(P_Vz)<F_m(z)$ whenever $z\notin V$. Thus every minimizer lies in $V$. The function $F_m$ is continuous and coercive because $F_m(z)\ge k\|z\|-\sum_j\|m_j\|$; its sublevel set $\{z\in V:F_m(z)\le F_m(0)\}$ is nonempty, closed and bounded in the finite-dimensional coordinate space $\mathbb R^d$, hence compact by [F3]. By [F5], $F_m$ attains a minimum there; the full minimizer set $C_m$ is nonempty, closed, bounded and compact, and it is convex because $F_m$ is convex.

By [F2], $C_m$ has a unique point $z_*(m)$ nearest to $0$, its unique minimum-norm point. If $H=\{0\}$, the selection is the constant zero map; otherwise fix a unit vector $e$ and a countable dense sequence $(d_a)_{a\ge1}$ in $H$, whose existence is given by [F8]. The countable set $D=\{\langle d_a,e\rangle:a\ge1\}$ is dense in $\mathbb R$: for each $t\in\mathbb R$, density gives $d_{a_j}\to te$, and [F4] gives $\langle d_{a_j},e\rangle\to t$. For $\lambda>0$, $G_{\lambda,m}(z)=F_m(z)+\lambda\|z\|^2$ is continuous, coercive and strictly convex. Projection to $V$ cannot increase $F_m$ and strictly decreases the squared norm off $V$, so every minimizer lies in $V$; if $d=0$ the single candidate is $0$. For $d>0$, a closed bounded sublevel set in $V$ is compact by [F3], so [F5] gives a unique minimizer $z_\lambda(m)$. By continuity and density, $h_\lambda(m)=\inf_aG_{\lambda,m}(d_a)=G_{\lambda,m}(z_\lambda(m))$. Each map $m\mapsto G_{\lambda,m}(d_a)$ is continuous, so [F7] makes their countable infimum $h_\lambda$ Borel. For $s\ge1$, set $A_{a,s}=\{m:G_{\lambda,m}(d_a)<h_\lambda(m)+1/s\}$. The countable dense set $D$ gives $A_{a,s}=\bigcup_{q\in D}\{m:G_{\lambda,m}(d_a)<q\}\cap\{m:h_\lambda(m)>q-1/s\}$ so $A_{a,s}$ is Borel; density ensures at least one such $a$ for each $m$. The least such $a$ is a Borel, countably-valued map because its level set at $a$ is $A_{a,s}\setminus\bigcup_{b<a}A_{b,s}$, and the selected point map is Borel since each open-set preimage is the union of its Borel level sets whose values lie in that open set. The selected point is within $(\lambda s)^{-1/2}$ of $z_\lambda(m)$: convexity of $F_m$ and $\|(1-t)z+ty\|^2=(1-t)\|z\|^2+t\|y\|^2-t(1-t)\|y-z\|^2$, applied at the minimizer and followed by $t\downarrow0$, give $G_{\lambda,m}(y)-G_{\lambda,m}(z_\lambda)\ge\lambda\|y-z_\lambda\|^2$. Hence the selected maps converge pointwise to $z_\lambda$. Since they are countably valued with Borel level sets, their distances to each $d_a$ are Borel and converge to $\|z_\lambda-d_a\|$; [F7] makes these limits Borel. Balls with centers $d_a$ and positive rational radii form a countable basis of the separable metric space $H$: every open neighborhood of a point contains such a ball around a sufficiently close dense center. Thus inverse images of open sets are countable unions of Borel inverse images of these balls, proving $m\mapsto z_\lambda(m)$ is Borel.

For every $s\ge1$, comparison with $z_*(m)$ in the minimization of $F_m+s^{-1}\|\cdot\|^2$ gives $\|z_{1/s}\|\le\|z_*\|$ and $F_m(z_{1/s})\le F_m(z_*)+s^{-1}\|z_*\|^2$. If $d=0$ then both points are $0$. Otherwise all $z_{1/s}$ lie in the compact ball $B_V(0,\|z_*\|)$ by [F3]. The closed tail sets $C_n=\overline{\{z_{1/s}:s\ge n\}}$ inside this ball are nonempty, nested and have the finite-intersection property, so [F6] gives $c\in\bigcap_n C_n$. For every $n$, continuity of $F_m$ and the tail bounds imply $F_m(c)\le F_m(z_*)+\|z_*\|^2/n$, while $\|c\|\le\|z_*\|$; letting $n\to\infty$ shows $c\in C_m$ is a minimum-norm minimizer, hence $c=z_*$. If the sequence did not converge to $z_*$, some $\rho>0$ would leave arbitrarily late terms at distance at least $\rho$; the closed tail closures of those terms are nonempty nested subsets of the same compact ball, so [F6] gives a point in their intersection. It lies in every $C_n$, hence equals $z_*$, but its distance from $z_*$ is at least $\rho$, a contradiction. Thus $z_{1/s}\to z_*$. By [F7] and the separable-metric basis argument of step 1.2, the pointwise limit of the Borel maps $z_{1/s}$ is Borel.

The minimizer set is nonempty, closed and convex by step 1.1, its minimum-norm point is unique by step 1.2, and step 2.1 proves the selected map is Borel. The only choice principle used is Countable Choice in [F2]; the dense sequence is supplied by separability and all subsequent approximations use least-index rules.

boundaries.evidence: Statement: k>=1 excludes an empty objective; step 1.1 obtains a nonempty compact sublevel set containing 0 and hence a nonempty minimizer set.
Step 1.1: when the center span has dimension zero, all centers are zero and F_m(z)=k||z|| has the unique minimizer 0.
Statement and step 1.1: k=1 makes the sole center the unique median and therefore the minimum-norm minimizer.
Step 1.2: even when the original median set contains many points, Hilbert projection chooses its unique nearest point to 0; regularization is strictly convex.
Step 2.1: the regularization parameters 1/s decrease to zero only through positive values; no assertion of strict convexity at lambda=0 is used.
Step 1.2 makes the approximation comparison sets Borel by a countable dense real-threshold formula and uses least-index rules; Countable Choice is retained only for F2 projection.

Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, let $n\ge1$, and let $1\le k\le n$ be an integer. Given $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in H^n$, put $q=\lfloor n/k\rfloor$ and $r=n-kq$. Form consecutive blocks $B_1,\ldots,B_k$ in index order, with $|B_j|=q+1$ for $j\le r$ and $|B_j|=q$ for $j>r$. Compute the block means $m_j=|B_j|^{-1}\sum_{i\in B_j}x_i$. Return the unique minimum-norm point of
$$
\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in H}\sum_{j=1}^k\|z-m_j\|.
$$

The objective minimizers are called geometric medians of the block means. The minimum-norm rule makes the output single-valued. Existence, uniqueness of that selected point, and Borel measurability as a function of the input tuple are proved in [[lem-measurable-minimum-norm-geometric-median-selection]].

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

derivations.claim: Suppose at most $ak$ points satisfy $\|m_j-z\|>r$. Since $C_a^2=1+a^2/(1-2a)>1$, write $D=\|z-m\|>C_a r>r$ and $d=(z-m)/D$. For each of the at least $(1-a)k$ remaining points, $u_j=(m_j-m)/\|m_j-m\|$ is defined and $\langle u_j,d\rangle\ge(D-\|m_j-z\|)/\|m_j-m\|>0$. Put $\cos\theta_j=\langle u_j,d\rangle$. By [F2], $0<\cos\theta_j\le1$; writing $d=\cos\theta_j u_j+w_j$ with $w_j\perp u_j$, Pythagoras gives $\|w_j\|=\sin\theta_j$. The distance from $z=m+Dd$ to the line through $m$ and $m_j$ is $D\|w_j\|=D\sin\theta_j$, and is at most $\|z-m_j\|\le r$. Therefore $\cos\theta_j\ge\sqrt{1-(r/D)^2}>\sqrt{1-C_a^{-2}}=a/(1-a)$.

For $m_j\ne m$, rationalizing the difference quotient gives $\lim_{t\downarrow0}(\|m+td-m_j\|-\|m-m_j\|)/t=\langle m-m_j,d\rangle/\|m-m_j\|=-\cos\theta_j$; if $m_j=m$, the quotient is $\|td\|/t=1$. Thus the right directional derivative of $F(m+td)$ is $-\sum_{m_j\ne m}\cos\theta_j+\#\{j:m_j=m\}$. Each good point from step 1.1 contributes less than $-a/(1-a)$, and each other point contributes at most $1$ by [F2]. Since at least $(1-a)k$ points are good, the derivative is strictly less than $k-(1-a)k(1+a/(1-a))=0$. At a minimizer every right difference quotient is nonnegative, so this negative derivative is impossible. Thus more than $ak$ points lie outside the radius-$r$ ball about $z$.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $C\subseteq H$ be nonempty, closed and convex, and let $x\in H$. Then there is exactly one point $p\in C$ with $\|x-p\|=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|$, that is, a unique nearest point of $C$ to $x$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix a separable real Hilbert space $H$ and an integer $k\ge1$. The rule in [[alg-geometric-median-of-block-means]] defines a single-valued Borel map $H^k\to H$: for every tuple $(m_1,\ldots,m_k)$ the function $F_m(z)=\sum_{j=1}^k\|z-m_j\|$ has a nonempty closed convex minimizer set, and that set has a unique point of minimum norm. The choice-free Borel construction below does not use weak compactness or reflexivity. Countable Choice is used only for the published Hilbert projection supplier that identifies the minimum-norm point.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

For $E\in\mathcal A$, write
$\int_Ef\,d\mu:=\int_\Omega\mathbf1_Ef\,d\mu$ whenever this function is
Bochner integrable.

Let $f:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable. Then $f$ is Bochner integrable if
and only if

$$\int_\Omega\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Here an a.e.-defined scalar function is integrated through any measurable
representative supplied by the strong simple approximation. Moreover the
Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

If $f:\Omega\to X$ is Bochner integrable, then for every measurable $E$,

$$\left\|\int_E f\,d\mu\right\|\leq\int_E\|f\|\,d\mu.$$

Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces, let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded and linear, and let $f$
be Bochner integrable. Then $T\circ f$ is Bochner integrable and, for every
measurable $E$,

$$T\left(\int_Ef\,d\mu\right)=\int_E Tf\,d\mu.$$

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of sigma-algebras on a
probability space, and let $J_0,\dots,J_{m-1}\subseteq I$ be pairwise disjoint
index sets. For each $r<m$, define

$$\mathcal G_r:=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{i\in J_r}\mathcal F_i\right).$$

Then the sigma-algebras $\mathcal G_0,\dots,\mathcal G_{m-1}$ are independent.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

$$
If $z\in H$ satisfies $\|m-z\|>C_a r$, then more than $ak$ of the points $m_j$ satisfy $\|m_j-z\|>r$.

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

Let $A$ be a nonempty set. Then $A$ is at most countable ([[def-countable]]) if
and only if there is a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to A$

Moreover, from any such surjection an injection $A \to \mathbb{N}$ is obtained
explicitly, without any choice, by

$$j(a) := \min\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : s(k) = a \,\}.$$

This is the working form of countability used everywhere below: to prove a

avoided outright, because $\min$ is canonical: every nonempty set of naturals has
a *least* element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]), so $j(a)$ is determined by
$a$ and $s$ alone.

derivations.claim: The map $X_1$ is strongly measurable: by [F13], fix a countable dense sequence $(h_j)$ in $H$ and approximate each $x\in H$ by the nearest of $h_1,\ldots,h_m$, breaking finite ties by the least index. The cells defining these finite-valued simple Borel maps are Borel because they are finite intersections of strict or weak comparisons of continuous distance functions, and the maps converge pointwise to $x$. Since $\|X_1\|\le1+\|X_1\|^2$, $E\|X_1\|<\infty$, so [F1] defines $\mu=E_BX_1$.

If the geometric median is farther than $C_a r_0$ from $\mu$, [F9] forces more than $ak$ bad block means. For $W$ the number of bad blocks, independence and $P(\text{bad block }j)\le p$ give $E e^{\lambda W}\le(1-p+pe^\lambda)^k$ for $\lambda>0$. Markov's inequality with $\lambda=\log(a(1-p)/(p(1-a)))>0$ gives $P(W\ge ak)\le e^{-k\psi(a;p)}<\delta$, after substituting this $\lambda$ and simplifying.

For the rank-one operator $x\otimes y$, [F10] gives $\|x\otimes y\|\le\|x\|\|y\|$, with equality by testing $y/\|y\|$ when $y\ne0$; its only possible nonzero singular value is this operator norm, so $\|x\otimes y\|_1=\|x\|\|y\|$. Apply the rank-one map to the finite-valued simple approximants from step 1.1: the resulting $S_1(H)$-valued functions are simple and converge pointwise in trace norm, because $\|u\otimes u-v\otimes v\|_1\le(\|u\|+\|v\|)\|u-v\|$. Hence $(X_1-\mu)\otimes(X_1-\mu)$ is strongly measurable; its trace norm is $\|X_1-\mu\|^2$, which is integrable since $E\|X_1-\mu\|^2\le2E\|X_1\|^2+2\|\mu\|^2$. The Bochner integrability criterion gives its Bochner expectation $\Sigma$ in $S_1(H)$. The bounded trace functional commutes with this integral by [F3], and [F2] gives $\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=E\|X_1-\mu\|^2=V$. For $h,g\in H$, bounded evaluation maps commute with the integral and give $\langle\Sigma h,g\rangle=E[\langle h,X_1-\mu\rangle\langle X_1-\mu,g\rangle]$; this is symmetric in $h,g$ and is nonnegative when $h=g$. If $V=0$, [F11] gives $X_1=\mu$ almost surely. Identical distribution and a finite union of null events imply that all $X_i=\mu$ simultaneously almost surely; hence every block mean is $\mu$. The objective in [F12] is then $k\|z-\mu\|$, uniquely minimized at $\mu$, so $\widehat\mu=\mu$ almost surely. Thus the strict-tail event in the Statement is empty when its threshold is zero. Assume $V>0$ below.

Let $m_j^{\circ}$ be a block size. For centered $Y_i=X_i-\mu$, expand $E\|\sum_{i\in B_j}Y_i\|^2$ into diagonal and cross terms. Each diagonal term is $V$; for $i\ne l$, product-law independence [F4] and scalar Fubini [F6] give $E\langle Y_i,Y_l\rangle=\int\!\int\langle x,y\rangle\,dP_Y(x)dP_Y(y)=0$. The integrand is integrable because [F10] gives $|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\|y\|$ and $E\|Y_i\|<\infty$; the inner integral is zero by [F3] and $E_BY_l=0$. Dividing by $(m_j^{\circ})^2$ yields $E\|m_j-\mu\|^2=V/m_j^{\circ}$.

Since $k\le n/2$, every block has size at least $\lfloor n/k\rfloor\ge n/(2k)$. Put $r_0=\sqrt{2kV/(pn)}$. By [F5] and step 3.1, $P(\|m_j-\mu\|>r_0)\le p$ for each block. The block means are independent by [F4], and [F12] makes their geometric-median aggregate a Borel random element.

The same Chernoff calculation as step 1.2 applies to every $q<a$. For each sufficiently large integer $s$, use radius $(1-1/s)r_0$ in step 4.1, so the bad-block probability is at most $p_s=p/(1-1/s)^2<a$. The event $\{\|\widehat\mu-\mu\|\ge C_ar_0\}$ is contained in the corresponding strict-radius event, whose probability is at most $e^{-k\psi(a;p_s)}$. Let $s\to\infty$; continuity gives $e^{-k\psi(a;p)}<\delta$.

For $a=7/18$ and $p=1/10$, $C_a=(1-a)/\sqrt{1-2a}$; applying [L1] with $M=50$ and $t=-13/68,13/22,1/6$ gives $2915/10000<\psi(a;p)<2916/10000$ and $3364/10000<\log(7/5)$. Hence $5/18<\psi(a;p)<\log(7/5)$ and $C_a\sqrt{2/(p\psi(a;p))}\le11$. From $k=\lfloor\log(1/\delta)/\psi(a;p)\rfloor+1$ we have $k\psi(a;p)\le\log(1/\delta)+\psi(a;p)<\log(7/(5\delta))$. Step 4.1 therefore gives the asserted nonstrict-tail bound for $V>0$ after replacing $r_0$ by its expression; the strict-tail event is a subset, so its bound follows as well. When $V=0$, exact recovery in step 2.1 gives the strict-tail bound. No nonstrict-tail assertion at zero threshold is made.

supplier_excerpts.quote:
Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, let $n\ge1$, and let $1\le k\le n$ be an integer. Given $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in H^n$, put $q=\lfloor n/k\rfloor$ and $r=n-kq$. Form consecutive blocks $B_1,\ldots,B_k$ in index order, with $|B_j|=q+1$ for $j\le r$ and $|B_j|=q$ for $j>r$. Compute the block means $m_j=|B_j|^{-1}\sum_{i\in B_j}x_i$. Return the unique minimum-norm point of
$$
\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in H}\sum_{j=1}^k\|z-m_j\|.
$$

The objective minimizers are called geometric medians of the block means. The minimum-norm rule makes the output single-valued. Existence, uniqueness of that selected point, and Borel measurability as a function of the input tuple are proved in [[lem-measurable-minimum-norm-geometric-median-selection]].

Fix a separable real Hilbert space $H$ and an integer $k\ge1$. The rule in [[alg-geometric-median-of-block-means]] defines a single-valued Borel map $H^k\to H$: for every tuple $(m_1,\ldots,m_k)$ the function $F_m(z)=\sum_{j=1}^k\|z-m_j\|$ has a nonempty closed convex minimizer set, and that set has a unique point of minimum norm. The choice-free Borel construction below does not use weak compactness or reflexivity. Countable Choice is used only for the published Hilbert projection supplier that identifies the minimum-norm point.

Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space, let $m_1,\ldots,m_k\in H$, and let $m$ minimize $F(z)=\sum_{j=1}^k\|z-m_j\|$. For $0<a<1/2$ and $r>0$, put
$$
C_a=\frac{1-a}{\sqrt{1-2a}}.
$$
If $z\in H$ satisfies $\|m-z\|>C_a r$, then more than $ak$ of the points $m_j$ satisfy $\|m_j-z\|>r$.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

For $E\in\mathcal A$, write
$\int_Ef\,d\mu:=\int_\Omega\mathbf1_Ef\,d\mu$ whenever this function is
Bochner integrable.

Let $f:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable. Then $f$ is Bochner integrable if
and only if

$$\int_\Omega\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Here an a.e.-defined scalar function is integrated through any measurable
representative supplied by the strong simple approximation. Moreover the
Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
definition.

If $f:\Omega\to X$ is Bochner integrable, then for every measurable $E$,

$$\left\|\int_E f\,d\mu\right\|\leq\int_E\|f\|\,d\mu.$$

Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces, let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded and linear, and let $f$
be Bochner integrable. Then $T\circ f$ is Bochner integrable and, for every
measurable $E$,

$$T\left(\int_Ef\,d\mu\right)=\int_E Tf\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $C\subseteq H$ be nonempty, closed and convex, and let $x\in H$. Then there is exactly one point $p\in C$ with $\|x-p\|=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|$, that is, a unique nearest point of $C$ to $x$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of sigma-algebras on a
probability space, and let $J_0,\dots,J_{m-1}\subseteq I$ be pairwise disjoint
index sets. For each $r<m$, define

$$\mathcal G_r:=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{i\in J_r}\mathcal F_i\right).$$

Then the sigma-algebras $\mathcal G_0,\dots,\mathcal G_{m-1}$ are independent.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

Let $A$ be a nonempty set. Then $A$ is at most countable ([[def-countable]]) if
and only if there is a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to A$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

Moreover, from any such surjection an injection $A \to \mathbb{N}$ is obtained
explicitly, without any choice, by

$$j(a) := \min\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : s(k) = a \,\}.$$

This is the working form of countability used everywhere below: to prove a
nonempty set countable it suffices to list its elements, repetitions and all.

**No choice principle is used.** The backward direction is where an appeal to
choice would be natural ("for each $a$ pick some $k$ with $s(k) = a$") and it is
avoided outright, because $\min$ is canonical: every nonempty set of naturals has
a *least* element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]), so $j(a)$ is determined by
$a$ and $s$ alone.

supplier_excerpts.quote: Fix an integer $N\ge1$, $0<\varepsilon\le1/4$, and the split-sample rule in [[alg-univariate-trimmed-mean]]. It defines a total continuous, hence Borel measurable, map $\mathbb R^{2N}\to\mathbb R$ for every admissible pair of observed samples, including tied values.

citations.quote:
Let $Z$ be a real random variable whose law is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$. For $0<u<1$, define
$$
Q_u(Z)=\sup\{t\in\mathbb R:P(Z\ge t)\ge1-u\}.
$$
Then $Q_u(Z)$ is finite and
$$
P(Z\ge Q_u(Z))=P(Z>Q_u(Z))=1-u.
$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For a statistical experiment $\{P_\theta\}$ from [[def-statistical-experiment]], sample size $N\ge1$, and replacement fraction $0\le\eta\le1$, equip $\mathcal X^N$ with its finite product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). A sample-replacement coupling is a pair of $\mathcal X^N$-valued random elements on a common probability space ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]) $(X,Y)$ such that $X_1,\ldots,X_N$ are iid with law $P_\theta$ under [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]] and
$$
\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf1\{X_i\ne Y_i\}\le\lfloor\eta N\rfloor
$$
almost surely. Assume the diagonal $\Delta_{\mathcal X}=\{(x,x):x\in\mathcal X\}$ belongs to the product sigma-algebra $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A$ ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]), so each mismatch indicator is measurable. The joint law may depend on the entire clean sample; the observed vector $Y$ need not be iid.

Let $N\ge1$ be an integer, let $\eta\ge0$, $0<\delta<1$, and set
$$
\varepsilon=8\eta+\frac{12\log(4/\delta)}{N}.
$$
The procedure is admissible when $0<\varepsilon\le1/4$. Its input is two observed real samples $\widetilde X_1,\ldots,\widetilde X_N$ and $\widetilde Y_1,\ldots,\widetilde Y_N$. Sort the second sample nondecreasingly as $\widetilde Y^*_{(1)}\le\cdots\le\widetilde Y^*_{(N)}$ and define $r(u)=\lceil uN\rceil$ for $0<u\le1$. Set
$$
\alpha=\widetilde Y^*_{(r(\varepsilon))},\qquad \beta=\widetilde Y^*_{(r(1-\varepsilon))},
$$
and, for $\alpha\le\beta$, let $\phi_{\alpha,\beta}(x)=\min\{\beta,\max\{\alpha,x\}\}$. Return
$$
\widehat\mu=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\phi_{\alpha,\beta}(\widetilde X_i).
$$
The operation is defined for every admissible input, including tied observations.

Fix an integer $N\ge1$, $0<\varepsilon\le1/4$, and the split-sample rule in [[alg-univariate-trimmed-mean]]. It defines a total continuous, hence Borel measurable, map $\mathbb R^{2N}\to\mathbb R$ for every admissible pair of observed samples, including tied values.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent centered square-integrable real random variables. Suppose $b\ge0$ is finite and $|X_i|\le b$ almost surely for each $i$. Put $v=\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(X_i)$. For $t>0$, if $v>0$ then
$$\mathbb P\left(\left|\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right|\ge t\right)\le 2\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2(v+bt/3)}\right),$$
and if $v=0$ then this probability is $0$.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

For $p\in[0,1]$, a **Bernoulli$(p)$ random variable** takes the value $1$ with probability $p$ and $0$ with probability $1-p$.

For $n\in\mathbb N$, a **binomial$(n,p)$ random variable** is a sum $X=\sum_{i<n}X_i$ of $n$ mutually independent Bernoulli$(p)$ variables. When $n=0$, this is the constant zero random variable.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

derivations.claim: Shifting every clean and observed coordinate by $-\mu$ shifts both order-statistic cutoffs, every clipped value, and the output by $-\mu$, so it suffices to analyze the centered data $Z$. By [F1], for each $p\in(0,1)$ the quantile $q_p=Q_p(Z)$ has $P(Z\le q_p)=p$ and $P(Z\ge q_p)=1-p$. Thus $|q_p|\le\sigma/\sqrt{\min(p,1-p)}$: if $q_p\ge0$, use $\sigma^2\ge q_p^2P(Z\ge q_p)$; if $q_p<0$, use $\sigma^2\ge q_p^2P(Z\le q_p)$. For any event $A$, $E[|Z|\mathbf1_A]\le\sigma\sqrt{P(A)}$: when $P(A)>0$, this follows by expanding $0\le E[(|Z|/\sigma-\mathbf1_A/\sqrt{P(A)})^2]$, and the zero-probability case is immediate. Also $T$ is nondecreasing, since its tail sets expand with $u$, and $T(4\varepsilon)\le\sigma\sqrt{2\varepsilon}$ by [F1] and this inequality. For a lower clipping endpoint $a=q_p$ with $p\le1/2$, put $L=E[|Z|\mathbf1_{\{Z\le a\}}]$. If $a\le0$, $E[(a-Z)\mathbf1_{\{Z\le a\}}]\le L$. If $a>0$, centering implies $a(1-p)\le E[Z\mathbf1_{\{Z>a\}}]=-E[Z\mathbf1_{\{Z\le a\}}]\le L$; hence $ap\le L$ and the clipping excess is at most $2L$. The symmetric upper-endpoint argument is identical. For a deterministic clip $W=\phi_{a,b}(Z)$, $E[(W-c)^2]=\operatorname{Var}W+(EW-c)^2$ with $c=\phi_{a,b}(0)$, and $|W-c|\le|Z|$ because clipping is 1-Lipschitz. Thus $\operatorname{Var}W\le\sigma^2$; also $|W-EW|\le b-a$ since both values lie in $[a,b]$.

First use inner endpoints $q_{2\varepsilon},q_{1-2\varepsilon}$ and outer endpoints $q_{\varepsilon/2},q_{1-\varepsilon/2}$. Require each of the two inner clean $Y$ tail counts to exceed $N(\varepsilon+2\eta)$ and each outer count to be less than $N(\varepsilon-2\eta)$. Put $a=\eta/t\ge0$. Since $\varepsilon=(8a+12)t$, [F3] for the binomial counts bounds each inner failure by $\exp[-36(a+2)^2\ell/(36a+56)]\le e^{-18\ell/7}$, and each outer failure by $\exp[-(2a+6)^2\ell/((28/3)a+16)]\le e^{-9\ell/4}$. The two rational functions are increasing for $a\ge0$, as direct differentiation shows, so their minima are their values at zero. Thus all four count conditions hold outside probability $4e^{-9\ell/4}\le\delta/2$, since $\ell>\log4$. After $M\le2\eta N$ changes the inner counts are still strictly greater than $\varepsilon N$ and outer counts strictly less than $\varepsilon N$. Integer counts and the ranks $r_-=\lceil\varepsilon N\rceil$, $r_+=N-\lfloor\varepsilon N\rfloor$ therefore give $q_{\varepsilon/2}\le\alpha-\mu\le q_{2\varepsilon}$ and $q_{1-2\varepsilon}\le\beta-\mu\le q_{1-\varepsilon/2}$. For example fewer than $\varepsilon N$ values below an outer lower endpoint means at most $r_--1$ such values, while more than $\varepsilon N$ values above an inner upper endpoint means at least $\lfloor\varepsilon N\rfloor+1$ such values. These strict inequalities cover noninteger ranks and the integral boundary without a rounding loss.

On the count event, monotonicity of clipping endpoints bounds the clean first-half clipped average above by the average of $W^+=\phi_{q_{2\varepsilon},q_{1-\varepsilon/2}}(Z)$ and below by the average of $W^-=\phi_{q_{\varepsilon/2},q_{1-2\varepsilon}}(Z)$. Step 1.1 bounds $EW^+\le2T(4\varepsilon)$ and $EW^-\ge-2T(4\varepsilon)$, their variances by $\sigma^2$, and their interval widths by $2\sqrt2\sigma/\sqrt\varepsilon$. These comparison variables have fixed endpoints, so their deviation events are functions of the clean $X$ half and do not rely on the corrupted cutoffs being independent of it. Apply [F3] at $a=\ell$ separately to the two comparisons. As $t/\varepsilon\le1/12$, each deviation is at most $\sigma\sqrt t[\sqrt2+(4\sqrt2/3)\sqrt{t/\varepsilon}]\le2\sigma\sqrt t$. Their total exceptional probability is $2e^{-\ell}=\delta/2$.

Write $A=q_{\varepsilon/2}$, $B=q_{1-\varepsilon/2}$. Replacing at most $M$ first-half points changes the clipped average by at most $2\eta(B-A)\le(\varepsilon/4)(B-A)$. If $A\le0\le B$, $(\varepsilon/4)(B-A)\le\max\{(\varepsilon/2)|A|,(\varepsilon/2)|B|\}\le T(\varepsilon)$. If both endpoints are positive, use $B-A\le B$ and the same upper-tail bound; if both are negative, use $B-A\le|A|$ and its lower-tail bound. By monotonicity $T(\varepsilon)\le T(4\varepsilon)$. Combining this with step 2.1 and the two exceptional probabilities proves the first displayed bound with its exact constants $3$ and $2$, uniformly over every admissible sample-dependent replacement.

For the second bound put $s=\varepsilon N/12\ge\ell>\log4$ and keep the same inner quantiles but use wider outer endpoints $q_{\varepsilon/4},q_{1-\varepsilon/4}$. Use the same count thresholds $N(\varepsilon\pm2\eta)$. Since $2\eta\le\varepsilon/4$, the inner downward gap is at least $3\varepsilon/4$ from mean $2\varepsilon$, and the outer upward gap is at least $\varepsilon/2$ from mean $\varepsilon/4$. The function $u^2/(2(p+u/3))$ increases for $u>0$, so [F3] bounds each inner failure by $e^{-\varepsilon N/8}=e^{-3s/2}$ and each outer failure by $e^{-3\varepsilon N/10}=e^{-18s/5}$. The same strict rank argument of step 1.2 brackets the corrupted cutoffs. For the fixed comparison clips, step 1.1 gives directional bias at most $2T(4\varepsilon)\le2\sqrt2\sigma\sqrt\varepsilon$, variance at most $\sigma^2$ and width at most $4\sigma/\sqrt\varepsilon$. Bernstein at $a=s$ therefore bounds each directional clean-average noise by $(1/\sqrt6+2/9)\sigma\sqrt\varepsilon$. The replacement shift is at most $2\eta\cdot4\sigma/\sqrt\varepsilon\le\sigma\sqrt\varepsilon$. The total error is consequently at most $(2\sqrt2+1/\sqrt6+2/9+1)\sigma\sqrt\varepsilon<10\sigma\sqrt\varepsilon$. Its exceptional probability is at most $2e^{-3s/2}+2e^{-18s/5}+2e^{-s}\le4e^{-s}$, because the first two terms sum to at most $4e^{-3s/2}\le2e^{-s}$. This proves the second assertion.

supplier_excerpts.quote:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. Give $\mathbb{R}^n$ its Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and its induced Euclidean metric $d_2$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $r>0$, put

$$\overline B_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2\le r\},\qquad S_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2=r\}.$$

These are respectively the **Euclidean closed ball** and **Euclidean sphere** with centre $c$ and radius $r$. They carry the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Since $d_2(c,x)=\lVert x-c\rVert_2$, they are precisely the closed ball and sphere $\bar B(c,r)$ and $S(c,r)$ of the metric-space definition ([[def-metric-ball]]).

For the unit sphere centred at the origin write

$$S^{n-1}:=S_2(0,1).$$

The exponent is notation for this particular sphere, not a claim that a dimension theory has been developed here.

For each fixed admissible $d,N,\varepsilon$ and each observed data tuple in $(\mathbb R^d)^{2N}$, the procedure [[alg-multivariate-trimmed-mean]] returns a unique vector in $\mathbb R^d$. As a function of the observed data tuple it is Borel measurable. The fallback branch covers the case where no dyadic tail intersection is nonempty; the all-scale branch covers the case where every tail intersection is nonempty.
