Let $d,N\ge1$ be integers, let $0\le\eta\le1/10$, and let $0<\delta<1$ satisfy $N\ge2560\log(2/\delta)$. Given two observed halves $\widetilde X_1,\ldots,\widetilde X_N$ and $\widetilde Y_1,\ldots,\widetilde Y_N$ in $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$
\varepsilon=\max\left\{10\eta,\frac{2560\log(2/\delta)}{N}\right\}\in(0,1].
$$
For $v\in S^{d-1}$, sort $\langle\widetilde Y_i,v\rangle$ nondecreasingly and let $\alpha_v$ and $\beta_v$ be its order statistics of ranks $\lceil\varepsilon N/2\rceil$ and $\lceil(1-\varepsilon/2)N\rceil$. Write $\phi_{a,b}(t)=\min\{b,\max\{a,t\}\}$. For $Q>0$ define
$$U_Q(v)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\phi_{\alpha_v-Q,\,\beta_v+Q}(\langle\widetilde X_i,v\rangle),\qquad \Gamma(v,Q)=\{z\in\mathbb R^d:|\langle z,v\rangle-U_Q(v)|\le2\varepsilon Q\}.$$
and $\Gamma(Q)=\bigcap_{v\in S^{d-1}}\Gamma(v,Q)$. For each $j\in\mathbb Z$, put
$$
K_j=\bigcap_{i\ge j}\Gamma(2^i),\qquad S=\{j\in\mathbb Z:K_j\ne\varnothing\}.
$$
Return the unique minimum-norm point of $K_j$ if $S$ has least element $j$; if $S=\mathbb Z$, return the unique minimum-norm point of $\bigcap_{i\in\mathbb Z}\Gamma(2^i)$; if $S=\varnothing$, return the first-half sample mean $N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\widetilde X_i$. This three-branch selector is total on the displayed input domain; its existence and Borel measurability are proved in [[lem-multivariate-trimmed-mean-selector-total-and-measurable]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. Give $\mathbb{R}^n$ its Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and its induced Euclidean metric $d_2$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $r>0$, put

$$\overline B_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2\le r\},\qquad S_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2=r\}.$$

These are respectively the **Euclidean closed ball** and **Euclidean sphere** with centre $c$ and radius $r$. They carry the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Since $d_2(c,x)=\lVert x-c\rVert_2$, they are precisely the closed ball and sphere $\bar B(c,r)$ and $S(c,r)$ of the metric-space definition ([[def-metric-ball]]).

For the unit sphere centred at the origin write

$$S^{n-1}:=S_2(0,1).$$

The exponent is notation for this particular sphere, not a claim that a dimension theory has been developed here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), and let $\mathbb{R}$ carry its usual topology, the
metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. **Continuous images.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous
   ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) and $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact
   ([[def-compact-space]]), then $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. More
   generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$ then $f[K]$ is a
   compact subset of $Y$.
2. **Extreme values.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact and nonempty and
   $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g[X]$ has a maximum and a minimum
   ([[def-max-min]]): there are $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with
   $$g(x_{\min}) \;\le\; g(x) \;\le\; g(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X .$$
3. **Compact to Hausdorff.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact, $(Y,
   \mathcal{T}_Y)$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $f : X \to Y$ is a
   continuous bijection, then $f$ is a homeomorphism
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

Nonemptiness in claim 2 is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for
$X = \varnothing$ the image is empty and has neither a maximum nor a minimum. **No
choice principle is used**: the one selection made below is over a finite index
set, where [[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. Give $\mathbb{R}^n$ its Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and its induced Euclidean metric $d_2$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $r>0$, put

$$\overline B_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2\le r\},\qquad S_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2=r\}.$$

These are respectively the **Euclidean closed ball** and **Euclidean sphere** with centre $c$ and radius $r$. They carry the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Since $d_2(c,x)=\lVert x-c\rVert_2$, they are precisely the closed ball and sphere $\bar B(c,r)$ and $S(c,r)$ of the metric-space definition ([[def-metric-ball]]).

For the unit sphere centred at the origin write

$$S^{n-1}:=S_2(0,1).$$

The exponent is notation for this particular sphere, not a claim that a dimension theory has been developed here.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with closed sets as in
[[def-metric-topology]] and the finite intersection property as in
[[def-finite-intersection-property]]. For a family $\mathcal{A}$ of subsets of
$X$ write

$$\bigcap \mathcal{A} \;:=\; \{\, x \in X : x \in F \text{ for every } F \in \mathcal{A} \,\},$$

so that $\bigcap \emptyset = X$, matching the convention for the empty finite
intersection in [[def-finite-intersection-property]].

Then $(X,d)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]) **if and only if** every
family $\mathcal{A}$ of closed subsets of $X$ with the finite intersection
property satisfies $\bigcap \mathcal{A} \ne \emptyset$.

No choice principle is used in either direction: complementation is a canonical
bijection, so no member of a family ever has to be selected.

Let $n\ge1$. The set $\mathbb Q^n$ is countable and dense in $\mathbb R^n$. Moreover the rational open boxes

$$\prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i),\qquad a_i,b_i\in\mathbb Q,\quad a_i<b_i,$$

form a countable basis for the product topology on $\mathbb R^n$.

Let $A$ be a nonempty set. Then $A$ is at most countable ([[def-countable]]) if
and only if there is a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to A$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

Moreover, from any such surjection an injection $A \to \mathbb{N}$ is obtained
explicitly, without any choice, by

$$j(a) := \min\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : s(k) = a \,\}.$$

This is the working form of countability used everywhere below: to prove a
nonempty set countable it suffices to list its elements, repetitions and all.

**No choice principle is used.** The backward direction is where an appeal to
choice would be natural ("for each $a$ pick some $k$ with $s(k) = a$") and it is
avoided outright, because $\min$ is canonical: every nonempty set of naturals has
a *least* element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]), so $j(a)$ is determined by
$a$ and $s$ alone.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

Let $n\ge1$. The set $\mathbb Q^n$ is countable and dense in $\mathbb R^n$. Moreover the rational open boxes

$$\prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i),\qquad a_i,b_i\in\mathbb Q,\quad a_i<b_i,$$

form a countable basis for the product topology on $\mathbb R^n$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

derivations.claim: Fix the data tuple $x$ and put $M(x)=\max_i\{\|\widetilde X_i\|_2,\|\widetilde Y_i\|_2\}$. Every projected observation and each order-statistic endpoint lies in $[-M(x),M(x)]$, so $|U_Q(v;x)|\le M(x)+Q$. Hence $z\in\Gamma(Q)$ implies $|\langle z,v\rangle|\le M(x)+(1+2\varepsilon)Q$ for every unit $v$ and $\|z\|_2\le M(x)+(1+2\varepsilon)Q$ by [F4]. Each order statistic of a finite list $a_1,\ldots,a_N$ equals $\min_{|J|=k}\max_{j\in J}a_j$ at rank $k$: every such maximum is at least the $k$th smallest entry, and the first $k$ indices attain it. Thus the directional order statistics, clipping endpoints, and $U_Q(v;x)$ are continuous in $(x,v)$ for fixed $Q$. Each $\Gamma(v,Q)$ is a closed convex slab; intersections preserve these properties. Therefore $\Gamma(Q)$ and every $K_j$ are closed and convex; a nonempty $K_j$ is bounded by the displayed radius at $Q=2^j$, hence compact by [F2].

Since $K_j\subseteq K_{j+1}$, $S=\{j:K_j\ne\varnothing\}$ is upward closed. If $S$ is nonempty and proper, choose $j_0\in S$ and $j_1\notin S$; upward closure forces $j_1<j_0$, and the least point of the nonempty finite set $S\cap\{j_1+1,\ldots,j_0\}$ is least in $S$. If $S=\mathbb Z$, the nested nonempty compact sets $K_0\supseteq K_{-1}\supseteq K_{-2}\supseteq\cdots$ have the finite-intersection property inside compact $K_0$, so [F5] gives a nonempty compact intersection. This intersection is exactly $\bigcap_{i\in\mathbb Z}\Gamma(2^i)$, since the constraints in $K_{-n}$ range over all $i\ge-n$. Each nonempty branch set (a least-index $K_j$ or the all-scale intersection) is compact and convex, so its norm attains a minimum by [F3]. If distinct $z,w$ both minimize squared norm, then $\|(z+w)/2\|_2^2=(\|z\|_2^2+\|w\|_2^2)/2-\|z-w\|_2^2/4$ is smaller, a contradiction; the minimum-norm point is unique. The empty-$S$ fallback is the defined first-half mean. Thus every branch is total and single-valued.

For fixed $Q>0$, define $g_Q(x,z)=\max_{v\in S^{d-1}}\{|\langle z,v\rangle-U_Q(v;x)|-2\varepsilon Q\}$. It is continuous: the maximand is jointly continuous by step 1.1, the sphere is compact by [F2], and on a compact neighborhood of any $(x,z)$ times the sphere [F8] gives uniform continuity, which bounds the change in the maximum by the supremum change of the maximand. Also, $\Gamma(Q)=\{z:g_Q(x,z)\le0\}$, and $g_Q$ is convex in $z$ as a maximum of absolute affine functions minus constants. Put $g_I(x,z)=\sup_{i\in I}g_{2^i}(x,z)$ for $I=I_j=\{i\in\mathbb Z:i\ge j\}$ or $I=\mathbb Z$. If $Q\ge2M(x)$, no first-half projection is clipped, so $U_Q(v;x)=\langle\bar X,v\rangle$ and $g_Q(x,z)=\|z-\bar X\|_2-2\varepsilon Q$, where $\bar X=N^{-1}\sum_i\widetilde X_i$. On any compact neighborhood of $(x,z)$ this identity makes the high-scale terms tend uniformly to $-\infty$; for $I_j$ they are eventually below $g_{2^j}$, and for $I=\mathbb Z$ eventually below $g_1$. Thus the high-scale supremum is locally a finite maximum. For the all-integer index set, define $g_0$ using clipping to $[\alpha_v,\beta_v]$ and no error allowance; the same compact-sphere maximum argument shows $g_0$ is continuous. Expanding both clipping endpoints by $Q$ changes each clipped observation by at most $Q$, so $|g_Q-g_0|\le(1+2\varepsilon)Q$ uniformly in $(x,z)$. On a compact neighborhood, all scales $i<-m$ therefore have supremum between $g_0$ and $g_0+(1+2\varepsilon)2^{-m}$, while for all sufficiently large $m$ the scales $i>m$ are below $g_1$. Hence $g_I$ is a local uniform limit of the continuous finite maxima $\max\{g_0,g_{2^i}:-m\le i\le m\}$ and is continuous. Being a supremum of convex functions, $g_I$ is convex in $z$.

For $I=I_j$, every $z\in K_j$ satisfies $\|z\|_2\le R_j(x)=M(x)+(1+2\varepsilon)2^j$ by step 1.1; for $I=\mathbb Z$, every feasible $z$ lies in $\Gamma(1)$ and has norm at most $R_\infty(x)=M(x)+1+2\varepsilon$. These radii are positive and continuous. Since $K_I(x)=\{z:g_I(x,z)\le0\}$, its nonemptiness is equivalent to $m_I(x)\le0$, where $m_I(x)=\min_{\|w\|_2\le1}g_I(x,R_I(x)w)$. The minimum exists by [F2], [F3]. It is continuous in $x$: on a compact neighborhood of any $x$, [F8] makes $(x,w)\mapsto g_I(x,R_I(x)w)$ uniformly continuous in $x$ uniformly over the compact unit ball, and the difference of two minima is bounded by the supremum of the corresponding function differences. Thus each event $\{x:K_I(x)\ne\varnothing\}=\{x:m_I(x)\le0\}$ is Borel.

Fix one such branch index set $I$ and write $R=R_I(x)$. By [F6], enumerate a countable dense rational subset $(r_a)$ of $\mathbb Q^d$ and set $d_a=r_a/\max\{1,\|r_a\|_2\}$. The radial map is continuous and is the identity on the unit ball, so $(d_a)$ is dense in that ball. Let $h_I(x,w)=g_I(x,Rw)$ and, for each integer $\lambda\ge1$, minimize $J_{\lambda,I}(x,w)=R^2\|w\|_2^2+\lambda\max\{h_I(x,w),0\}$ over $\|w\|_2\le1$. The function is jointly continuous and strictly convex in $w$: $h_I$ is convex by step 2.2, its positive part is convex, and $R>0$ makes the quadratic strictly convex. Compactness and [F3] give a unique minimizer $w_{\lambda,I}(x)$. The value $b_{\lambda,I}(x)=\inf_aJ_{\lambda,I}(x,d_a)$ is Borel as a countable infimum of continuous functions and equals the minimum by density and continuity. For each integer $s\ge1$, put $A_{a,s}=\{x:J_{\lambda,I}(x,d_a)<b_{\lambda,I}(x)+1/s\}$. The rational points in [F6] give $A_{a,s}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q}\{x:J_{\lambda,I}(x,d_a)<q\}\cap\{x:b_{\lambda,I}(x)>q-1/s\}$, so $A_{a,s}$ is Borel. Such indices exist by density; the least one's level set is $A_{a,s}\setminus\bigcup_{b<a}A_{b,s}$, and $x\mapsto d_{a(x,s)}$ is Borel because each open-set preimage is the union of the Borel level sets whose values lie in that open set. Strong convexity gives $J_{\lambda,I}(x,y)-J_{\lambda,I}(x,w_{\lambda,I})\ge R^2\|y-w_{\lambda,I}\|_2^2$: apply the quadratic identity $\|(1-t)w+ty\|_2^2=(1-t)\|w\|_2^2+t\|y\|_2^2-t(1-t)\|y-w\|_2^2$, convexity of the penalty, minimality, and let $t\downarrow0$. Hence $\|d_{a(x,s)}-w_{\lambda,I}(x)\|_2<1/(R\sqrt{s})$, so these Borel maps converge pointwise to $w_{\lambda,I}$. Each selected map is countably valued with Borel level sets, so its coordinate functions are Borel; [F7] makes their pointwise limits measurable. Rational open boxes form a countable basis by [F6], so $w_{\lambda,I}$ is Borel. For each coordinate $j$, the pair $(R_I(x),w_{\lambda,I,j}(x))$ is Borel because inverse images of rational rectangles are intersections of coordinate preimages and those rectangles form a countable basis of $\mathbb R^2$. Multiplication is continuous, so its composition with this pair map is Borel by the inverse-image definition; hence $z_{\lambda,I}(x)=R_I(x)w_{\lambda,I}(x)$ is Borel.

On the Borel event $E_I=\{x:K_I(x)\ne\varnothing\}$, let $z_*(x)$ be its unique minimum-norm point from step 2.1 and put $w_*=z_*/R$. Comparing the penalized minimum with the feasible $w_*$ gives $\|z_{\lambda,I}(x)\|_2\le\|z_*(x)\|_2$ and $\max\{g_I(x,z_{\lambda,I}(x)),0\}\le\|z_*(x)\|_2^2/\lambda$. The sequence $z_{\lambda,I}(x)$ lies in the compact closed ball of radius $R(x)$ by [F2]. Every sequence in a compact metric space has a convergent subsequence: if no point had infinitely many terms in every neighborhood, neighborhoods containing only finitely many term indices would cover the ball, contradicting a finite subcover; if one point did have infinitely many terms in every neighborhood, choosing the least successive indices in shrinking balls would give a convergent subsequence. Thus every subsequence has a convergent subsubsequence. By continuity of $g_I$, each cluster point is feasible; the norm bound makes its norm no greater than $\|z_*(x)\|_2$, so uniqueness in step 2.1 forces every cluster point to equal $z_*(x)$. The full sequence therefore converges to $z_*(x)$: otherwise a subsequence staying a fixed positive distance away would have a different cluster point. The maps equal to $z_{\lambda,I}$ on $E_I$ and $0$ off it are Borel: for an open set their inverse image is the branch-event intersection with the Borel inverse image under $z_{\lambda,I}$, with $E_I^c$ added exactly when $0$ belongs to the open set. They converge everywhere, to $z_*$ on $E_I$ and to $0$ off it; their pointwise limit is Borel by [F7].

The events $S=\varnothing$, $S=\mathbb Z$, and $\min S=j$ are respectively countable intersections or combinations of the Borel nonemptiness events in step 3.1, so they are Borel by [F7]. On each such event the algorithm uses the corresponding Borel branch selector from step 5.1 or the continuous first-half mean. For every open target set, its inverse image under the piecewise map is the countable union of each branch event intersected with that branch map's Borel inverse image; it is Borel. Step 2.1 proves all branches defined and single-valued, so the complete output map is total and Borel.

Let $d,N\ge1$ be integers, let $0\le\eta\le1/10$, and let $0<\delta<1$ satisfy $N\ge2560\log(2/\delta)$. Given two observed halves $\widetilde X_1,\ldots,\widetilde X_N$ and $\widetilde Y_1,\ldots,\widetilde Y_N$ in $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$
\varepsilon=\max\left\{10\eta,\frac{2560\log(2/\delta)}{N}\right\}\in(0,1].
$$
For $v\in S^{d-1}$, sort $\langle\widetilde Y_i,v\rangle$ nondecreasingly and let $\alpha_v$ and $\beta_v$ be its order statistics of ranks $\lceil\varepsilon N/2\rceil$ and $\lceil(1-\varepsilon/2)N\rceil$. Write $\phi_{a,b}(t)=\min\{b,\max\{a,t\}\}$. For $Q>0$ define
$$U_Q(v)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\phi_{\alpha_v-Q,\,\beta_v+Q}(\langle\widetilde X_i,v\rangle),\qquad \Gamma(v,Q)=\{z\in\mathbb R^d:|\langle z,v\rangle-U_Q(v)|\le2\varepsilon Q\}.$$
and $\Gamma(Q)=\bigcap_{v\in S^{d-1}}\Gamma(v,Q)$. For each $j\in\mathbb Z$, put
$$
K_j=\bigcap_{i\ge j}\Gamma(2^i),\qquad S=\{j\in\mathbb Z:K_j\ne\varnothing\}.
$$

5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. Give $\mathbb{R}^n$ its Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and its induced Euclidean metric $d_2$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $r>0$, put

$$\overline B_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2\le r\},\qquad S_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2=r\}.$$

These are respectively the **Euclidean closed ball** and **Euclidean sphere** with centre $c$ and radius $r$. They carry the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Since $d_2(c,x)=\lVert x-c\rVert_2$, they are precisely the closed ball and sphere $\bar B(c,r)$ and $S(c,r)$ of the metric-space definition ([[def-metric-ball]]).

For the unit sphere centred at the origin write

$$S^{n-1}:=S_2(0,1).$$

The exponent is notation for this particular sphere, not a claim that a dimension theory has been developed here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open sets as in
[[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]].

- An **open cover** of $(X,d)$ is a family $\mathcal{U}$ of open subsets of $X$
  with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$, where
  $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily
  $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$ that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \emptyset$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,d)$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite subcover: for
  every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \emptyset$ and the empty subfamily
  covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the metric
  subspace $(A, d_A)$ is a compact metric space, $d_A$ being the restriction of
  $d$ to $A \times A$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A,d_A)$ and its own open sets, not
about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do agree,
but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]], and no item of this library may use the
ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading as the
definition is what makes "compact" a property of the metric space $(A,d_A)$
alone, so that a set compact in one ambient space is compact in every other one
containing it isometrically.

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. The
one-point space is compact too, and so is every space listed as
$\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$: given a cover, each $x_i$ lies in some member, and
finitely many members chosen in this way already cover.

**The finiteness convention, and how it is used both ways.** "Finite" above is
the listing form, matching the finite lists of
[[def-finite-intersection-property]]. It agrees with the definition of
finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number ([[def-countable]]), and
both directions of the agreement are available and are used below:

- A nonempty finite set $F$ in the sense of [[def-countable]] satisfies
  $F \approx m$ for some $m \ge 1$, and a bijection $m \to F$ is exactly a
  listing $F = \{a_0, \dots, a_{m-1}\}$.
- Conversely a set listed as $A = \{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$, that is the image of a
  function $a$ with domain $\sigma(n)$, is finite in the sense of
  [[def-countable]]: the map sending $x \in A$ to the least $i \le n$ with
  $a_i = x$ is an injection of $A$ into $\sigma(n)$, so $A$ is equinumerous with
  a subset of $\mathbb{N}$ bounded above, and such a subset is finite
  ([[lem-subset-of-countable]]).

Neither direction uses a choice principle: the second selects nothing, taking a
least index instead.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), and let $\mathbb{R}$ carry its usual topology, the
metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. **Continuous images.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous
   ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) and $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact
   ([[def-compact-space]]), then $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. More
   generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$ then $f[K]$ is a
   compact subset of $Y$.
2. **Extreme values.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact and nonempty and
   $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g[X]$ has a maximum and a minimum
   ([[def-max-min]]): there are $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with
   $$g(x_{\min}) \;\le\; g(x) \;\le\; g(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X .$$
3. **Compact to Hausdorff.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact, $(Y,
   \mathcal{T}_Y)$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $f : X \to Y$ is a
   continuous bijection, then $f$ is a homeomorphism
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

Nonemptiness in claim 2 is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for
$X = \varnothing$ the image is empty and has neither a maximum nor a minimum. **No
choice principle is used**: the one selection made below is over a finite index
set, where [[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with closed sets as in
[[def-metric-topology]] and the finite intersection property as in
[[def-finite-intersection-property]]. For a family $\mathcal{A}$ of subsets of
$X$ write

$$\bigcap \mathcal{A} \;:=\; \{\, x \in X : x \in F \text{ for every } F \in \mathcal{A} \,\},$$

so that $\bigcap \emptyset = X$, matching the convention for the empty finite
intersection in [[def-finite-intersection-property]].

Then $(X,d)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]) **if and only if** every
family $\mathcal{A}$ of closed subsets of $X$ with the finite intersection
property satisfies $\bigcap \mathcal{A} \ne \emptyset$.

No choice principle is used in either direction: complementation is a canonical
bijection, so no member of a family ever has to be selected.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

Let $n\ge1$. The set $\mathbb Q^n$ is countable and dense in $\mathbb R^n$. Moreover the rational open boxes

$$\prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i),\qquad a_i,b_i\in\mathbb Q,\quad a_i<b_i,$$

form a countable basis for the product topology on $\mathbb R^n$.

Let $A$ be a nonempty set. Then $A$ is at most countable ([[def-countable]]) if
and only if there is a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to A$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

Moreover, from any such surjection an injection $A \to \mathbb{N}$ is obtained
explicitly, without any choice, by

$$j(a) := \min\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : s(k) = a \,\}.$$

This is the working form of countability used everywhere below: to prove a
nonempty set countable it suffices to list its elements, repetitions and all.

**No choice principle is used.** The backward direction is where an appeal to
choice would be natural ("for each $a$ pick some $k$ with $s(k) = a$") and it is
avoided outright, because $\min$ is canonical: every nonempty set of naturals has
a *least* element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]), so $j(a)$ is determined by
$a$ and $s$ alone.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

risk_review.notes: Steps 1.1–6.1 reviewed against exact preimage and algorithm. Finite min-max order-statistic formula is continuous even at ties; all feasible sets are convex closed and norm bounded. Upward-closed S has precisely the empty/all/least-integer cases; nested compact sets make the all-scale branch nonempty. g_Q is continuous by compact-sphere uniformity; high Q>=2M yields norm(z-barX)-2epsilon Q and local finite maximum. Low-scale |g_Q-g_0|<=(1+2epsilon)Q gives a uniform limit, hence continuous g_I. Positive continuous R turns nonemptiness into a compact-ball minimum <=0. Strictly convex penalties and dense least-index approximants are Borel and converge to the unique minimum-norm feasible point. Compactness proof selects least sequence indices; no arbitrary choice. epsilon=1 tied rank case and M=0 covered. Reader additions spell out elementary comparison/product measurability and sequential compactness; no overstrong current assertion or substantial unmet prerequisite found.

citations.quote:
Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid with law $P$, $n\ge1$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a finite or countable class of measurable real functions containing $0$. Suppose $|f|\le B$ everywhere and $Pf^2\le s^2$ for all $f\in\mathcal F$, with finite $B,s\ge0$. Put
$$Z=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\sum_{i=1}^n(f(X_i)-Pf),\qquad W=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i)^2,\qquad m=EW.$$
For every $x>0$,
$$P\left(Z>EZ+2\sqrt{(8m+4ns^2)x}+\sqrt8\,Bx\right)\le e^{-x}.$$
The bound uses second moments, not only variances. All suprema are measurable by countability. No choice axiom is assumed.

Let $n\ge1$, let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID observations with law $P$, and let $Z_1',\ldots,Z_n'$ be an independent IID copy. Let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n$ be independent uniform signs, independent of both samples. Let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty countable class of measurable $P$-integrable real functions. Assume the two suprema below are finite almost surely. If $\Phi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ is finite, convex, and nondecreasing, then

$$\mathbb E\Phi\!\left(\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\left|\sum_{i=1}^n(f(Z_i)-Pf)\right|\right)\le \mathbb E\Phi\!\left(2\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\left|\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i f(Z_i)\right|\right).$$

The same statement holds for an uncountable class when a specified countable subclass gives the same three displayed suprema almost surely for the data, copy, and signs. This is an expectation inequality only; a tail form requires separate assumptions.

Let $m\ge1$, let $z_1,\ldots,z_m$ be fixed, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty finite class of real-valued functions on their domain. For each $i$, let $\Phi_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $|\Phi_i(x)-\Phi_i(y)|\le L|x-y|$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb R$, with a common $L\ge0$. Then

$$\frac1m\,\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i\Phi_i(f(z_i))\le L\,\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal F).$$

Equivalently, the unnormalized left expectation is at most $L$ times the unnormalized one-sided supremum on the right.

The same holds for a countable class when both suprema are finite for every sign vector. No condition $\Phi_i(0)=0$ is required; additive constants cancel because the proof compares coordinate differences.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $X$ be a Borel random vector in $\mathbb R^d$ with $E\|X\|_2^2<\infty$. Define $\mu=EX$ coordinatewise, $Y=X-\mu$, and the finite matrix $\Sigma$ by $\Sigma_{rs}=E[Y_rY_s]$ for $1\le r,s\le d$. Then $\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite,
$$
\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=E\|X-\mu\|_2^2,
$$
and $0\le\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\le\operatorname{tr}\Sigma$. If $\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=0$, then $X=\mu$ almost surely.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $d,N\ge1$ be integers, let $0\le\eta\le1/10$, and let $0<\delta<1$ satisfy $N\ge2560\log(2/\delta)$. Given two observed halves $\widetilde X_1,\ldots,\widetilde X_N$ and $\widetilde Y_1,\ldots,\widetilde Y_N$ in $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$
\varepsilon=\max\left\{10\eta,\frac{2560\log(2/\delta)}{N}\right\}\in(0,1].
$$
For $v\in S^{d-1}$, sort $\langle\widetilde Y_i,v\rangle$ nondecreasingly and let $\alpha_v$ and $\beta_v$ be its order statistics of ranks $\lceil\varepsilon N/2\rceil$ and $\lceil(1-\varepsilon/2)N\rceil$. Write $\phi_{a,b}(t)=\min\{b,\max\{a,t\}\}$. For $Q>0$ define
$$U_Q(v)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\phi_{\alpha_v-Q,\,\beta_v+Q}(\langle\widetilde X_i,v\rangle),\qquad \Gamma(v,Q)=\{z\in\mathbb R^d:|\langle z,v\rangle-U_Q(v)|\le2\varepsilon Q\}.$$
and $\Gamma(Q)=\bigcap_{v\in S^{d-1}}\Gamma(v,Q)$. For each $j\in\mathbb Z$, put
$$
K_j=\bigcap_{i\ge j}\Gamma(2^i),\qquad S=\{j\in\mathbb Z:K_j\ne\varnothing\}.
$$
Return the unique minimum-norm point of $K_j$ if $S$ has least element $j$; if $S=\mathbb Z$, return the unique minimum-norm point of $\bigcap_{i\in\mathbb Z}\Gamma(2^i)$; if $S=\varnothing$, return the first-half sample mean $N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\widetilde X_i$. This three-branch selector is total on the displayed input domain; its existence and Borel measurability are proved in [[lem-multivariate-trimmed-mean-selector-total-and-measurable]].

For a statistical experiment $\{P_\theta\}$ from [[def-statistical-experiment]], sample size $N\ge1$, and replacement fraction $0\le\eta\le1$, equip $\mathcal X^N$ with its finite product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). A sample-replacement coupling is a pair of $\mathcal X^N$-valued random elements on a common probability space ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]) $(X,Y)$ such that $X_1,\ldots,X_N$ are iid with law $P_\theta$ under [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]] and
$$
\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf1\{X_i\ne Y_i\}\le\lfloor\eta N\rfloor
$$
almost surely. Assume the diagonal $\Delta_{\mathcal X}=\{(x,x):x\in\mathcal X\}$ belongs to the product sigma-algebra $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A$ ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]), so each mismatch indicator is measurable. The joint law may depend on the entire clean sample; the observed vector $Y$ need not be iid.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$
For every real $a>0$, there is an integer $i$ such that $a\le2^i<2a$.

Let $n\ge1$. The set $\mathbb Q^n$ is countable and dense in $\mathbb R^n$. Moreover the rational open boxes

$$\prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i),\qquad a_i,b_i\in\mathbb Q,\quad a_i<b_i,$$

form a countable basis for the product topology on $\mathbb R^n$.

derivations.claim: Put $D=\{q/\|q\|_2:q\in\mathbb Q^d\setminus\{0\}\}$ and include the zero vector. By [F6], $D$ is countable and dense in $S^{d-1}$: rational vectors approximate every unit vector, and normalization is continuous at nonzero vectors. For each bounded continuous scalar map used below, the sample sums and their population expectations are continuous in direction, the latter by [F5]. Thus their suprema over $D\cup\{0\}$ equal the full directional suprema and are measurable. For any such class $g_v$, use the independent clean half $Y_1,\ldots,Y_N$ as the ghost copy of $X_1,\ldots,X_N$; its product law and independence follow from [F5] and the iid hypothesis. When the same argument is applied to the $Y$ half, swap the roles of the two clean halves. Jensen gives $E\sup_v\sum_i(g_v(X_i)-Pg_v)\le E\sup_v\sum_i(g_v(X_i)-g_v(Y_i))$. Pair swapping inserts independent signs; separating the two halves gives at most $2E\sup_v\sum_i\sigma_i g_v(X_i)$. For an $L$-Lipschitz scalar map $\psi$, averaging one sign with arbitrary remaining offsets $A_v$ gives $\frac12\sup_{v,w}(A_v+A_w+\psi(t_v)-\psi(t_w))\le\frac12\sup_{v,w}(A_v+A_w+L|t_v-t_w|)$. Swapping $v,w$ shows that the final supremum equals the one with $L(t_v-t_w)$; successive coordinate replacements prove one-sided contraction with factor $L$. Countable limits follow by monotone convergence after subtracting one fixed candidate, or bounded convergence on the finite sign space for a fixed sample. Finally set $S=\sum_i\sigma_i(X_i-\mu)$. Independence of the signs gives $E\|S\|^2=N\operatorname{tr}\Sigma$. Since $u\le1+u^2$ for $u\ge0$, $E\|S\|<\infty$; then $0\le E(\|S\|-E\|S\|)^2=E\|S\|^2-(E\|S\|)^2$ gives $E\|N^{-1}S\|\le r$.

Put $h(t)=\min\{1,(2|t|/Q_0-1)_+\}$. It is $2/Q_0$-Lipschitz, vanishes at zero and majorizes $\mathbf1_{\{|t|\ge Q_0\}}$. By [F3], $Ph(\langle X-\mu,v\rangle)\le4\lambda/Q_0^2\le\varepsilon/64$. For its centered supremum, step 1.1 gives $EZ/N\le4r/Q_0\le\varepsilon/64$. Since $h^2\le h$, $EW/N\le\varepsilon/32$, and its second moment is at most $\varepsilon/64$. Apply [F1] separately to each clean half with $B=1$. Except on probability $e^{-x}$ for each half, its maximal empirical $h$ average is at most $\varepsilon/32+2\sqrt{5\varepsilon x/(16N)}+\sqrt8 x/N=\varepsilon/16+\sqrt8\varepsilon/1280<\varepsilon/8$. Thus each clean half has fewer than $\varepsilon N/8$ projections of centered absolute value at least $Q_0$, uniformly in direction.

Fix $Q=2^{i_0}\in[2Q_0,4Q_0)$. Put $g_v(z)=\phi_{-Q,Q}(\langle z-\mu,v\rangle)$ and $W_Q(v)=N^{-1}\sum_i g_v(X_i)$. Antipodal directions and odd clipping make the absolute centered supremum equal its one-sided counterpart. Step 1.1 gives $EZ/N\le2r$. The square of clipping is $2Q$-Lipschitz and vanishes at zero, so the same symmetrization/contraction argument yields $EW/N\le\lambda+4Qr$ for the squared-class supremum. Here $|g_v|\le Q$ and $Pg_v^2\le\lambda$. Since $r\le\varepsilon Q/512$ and $\lambda\le\varepsilon Q^2/1024$, [F1] bounds $\sup_v|W_Q(v)-PW_Q(v)|$ outside probability $e^{-x}$ by $2r+2\sqrt{19\varepsilon Q^2x/(256N)}+\sqrt8 Qx/N<\varepsilon Q/32$. Also $|Pg_v|\le E[|\langle X-\mu,v\rangle|\mathbf1_{\{|\langle X-\mu,v\rangle|>Q\}}]\le\lambda/Q\le\varepsilon Q/1024$, since the unclipped projection is centered.

Each observed half has at most $2\eta N\le\varepsilon N/5$ changes. On both events of step 2.1, fewer than $13\varepsilon N/40<\varepsilon N/2$ projections in either observed half are outside $[\langle\mu,v\rangle-Q_0,\langle\mu,v\rangle+Q_0]$. Both directional quantile ranks $k=\lceil\varepsilon N/2\rceil$ and $k=\lceil(1-\varepsilon/2)N\rceil$ satisfy $k\ge\varepsilon N/2$ and $N-k+1\ge\varepsilon N/2$; in the potentially integral boundary the strict count inequality suffices. Hence both quantiles lie in that interval, including at $\varepsilon=1$. Write $a_v=\alpha_v-\langle\mu,v\rangle$ and $b_v=\beta_v-\langle\mu,v\rangle$, so $-Q_0\le a_v\le b_v\le Q_0$.

For any clean centered projection $t$, the data-dependent clipping $\phi_{a_v-Q,b_v+Q}(t)$ differs from $\phi_{-Q,Q}(t)$ by at most $Q_0$ and agrees with it when $|t|<Q-Q_0$. Since $Q-Q_0\ge Q_0$, step 2.1 bounds the average difference by $\varepsilon Q_0/8\le\varepsilon Q/16$. The data-dependent clipping interval has length at most $2Q+2Q_0\le3Q$, so first-half replacements change its average by at most $6\eta Q\le3\varepsilon Q/5$. Combining these bounds with step 2.2 gives $\sup_v|U_Q(v)-\langle\mu,v\rangle|\le(3/5+1/16+1/32+1/1024)\varepsilon Q=3557\varepsilon Q/5120<\varepsilon Q$. Thus $\mu\in\Gamma(Q)$ and every $z\in\Gamma(Q)$ has $\|z-\mu\|\le3\varepsilon Q<12\varepsilon Q_0\le16\varepsilon Q_0$.

Let $X$ be an absolutely continuous random vector in $\mathbb R^d$ with mean $\mu$ and finite covariance matrix $\Sigma$ as defined in [[lem-finite-covariance-matrix-basic-properties]]. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_N,Y_1,\ldots,Y_N$ be $2N$ iid clean copies and let their observed replacement sample have at most $\lfloor2\eta N\rfloor$ changed coordinates in total. Assume $0\le\eta\le1/10$, $0<\delta<1$, $N\ge2560\log(2/\delta)$, and $\varepsilon=\max\{10\eta,2560\log(2/\delta)/N\}\le1$. If $\operatorname{tr}\Sigma>0$, put
$$
Q_0=\max\left\{\frac{256}{\varepsilon}\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{tr}\Sigma}{N}},\ 16\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)}{\varepsilon}}\right\}.
$$
For the slabs and tail intersections in [[alg-multivariate-trimmed-mean]], [[lem-positive-real-has-dyadic-scale-in-factor-two]] supplies an integer $i_0$ with $2^{i_0}\in[2Q_0,4Q_0)$. Then, with probability at least $1-\delta$, $K_{i_0}=\bigcap_{i\ge i_0}\Gamma(2^i)$ is nonempty and every $z\in K_{i_0}$ satisfies $\|z-\mu\|\le16\varepsilon Q_0$. The positive-trace condition is required to make $Q_0>0$.

Let $\Sigma$ be a finite covariance matrix in $\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, with $\operatorname{tr}\Sigma>0$, mean $\mu$, and $0\le\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\le\operatorname{tr}\Sigma$ as in [[lem-finite-covariance-matrix-basic-properties]]. Let $0\le\eta\le1/10$, $0<\delta<1$, $N\ge2560\log(2/\delta)$, and $\varepsilon=\max\{10\eta,2560\log(2/\delta)/N\}$. Define
$$
Q_0=\max\left\{\frac{256}{\varepsilon}\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{tr}\Sigma}{N}},\ 16\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)}{\varepsilon}}\right\}.
$$
Fix $b>0$ and any integer $i_0$ with $2^{i_0}\in[2Q_0,4Q_0)$ and any observed input tuple to [[alg-multivariate-trimmed-mean]]. If $K_{i_0}$ is nonempty and every $z\in K_{i_0}$ satisfies $\|z-\mu\|_2\le b\varepsilon Q_0$, then the algorithm's output satisfies
$$
\|\widehat\mu-\mu\|_2\le c_b\left[\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{tr}\Sigma}{N}}+\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\log(1/\delta)}{N}}+\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\eta}\right],
$$
where
$$
c_b=b\max\left\{256+16\sqrt{2560\log2},\ 16\sqrt{2560},\ 16\sqrt{10}\right\}.
$$
In particular, $b=4$ recovers the original constant and $b=16$ applies to the corrected slab proposition. This is a deterministic implication from the slab event; it does not assert that the event has high probability.

Let $X$ be a Borel random vector in $\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, with finite second moment, mean $\mu$, and covariance matrix $\Sigma$ as defined in [[lem-finite-covariance-matrix-basic-properties]]. Let two halves of size $N$ be iid clean copies, and let the observed vector be a sample-replacement version with at most $\lfloor2\eta N\rfloor$ changed coordinates in total. Assume $0\le\eta\le1/10$, $0<\delta<1$, and $N\ge2560\log(2/\delta)$. With $\varepsilon=\max\{10\eta,2560\log(2/\delta)/N\}$, if $\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=0$, then [[alg-multivariate-trimmed-mean]] returns $\mu$ almost surely.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $X$ be a Borel random vector in $\mathbb R^d$ with $E\|X\|_2^2<\infty$. Define $\mu=EX$ coordinatewise, $Y=X-\mu$, and the finite matrix $\Sigma$ by $\Sigma_{rs}=E[Y_rY_s]$ for $1\le r,s\le d$. Then $\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite,
$$

$$
and $0\le\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\le\operatorname{tr}\Sigma$. If $\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=0$, then $X=\mu$ almost surely.

Let $d,N\ge1$ be integers, let $0\le\eta\le1/10$, and let $0<\delta<1$ satisfy $N\ge2560\log(2/\delta)$. Given two observed halves $\widetilde X_1,\ldots,\widetilde X_N$ and $\widetilde Y_1,\ldots,\widetilde Y_N$ in $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$

For $v\in S^{d-1}$, sort $\langle\widetilde Y_i,v\rangle$ nondecreasingly and let $\alpha_v$ and $\beta_v$ be its order statistics of ranks $\lceil\varepsilon N/2\rceil$ and $\lceil(1-\varepsilon/2)N\rceil$. Write $\phi_{a,b}(t)=\min\{b,\max\{a,t\}\}$. For $Q>0$ define
$$U_Q(v)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\phi_{\alpha_v-Q,\,\beta_v+Q}(\langle\widetilde X_i,v\rangle),\qquad \Gamma(v,Q)=\{z\in\mathbb R^d:|\langle z,v\rangle-U_Q(v)|\le2\varepsilon Q\}.$$
and $\Gamma(Q)=\bigcap_{v\in S^{d-1}}\Gamma(v,Q)$. For each $j\in\mathbb Z$, put
$$

Use the real random variable convention of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] and the expectation convention of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. A real random variable $X$ is **centered** when it is integrable and $\mathbb E X=0$. A vector random element $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_d)$ in $\mathbb R^d$, for an integer $d\ge1$, is centered when each coordinate is integrable and $\mathbb E Z_j=0$. For $u,z\in\mathbb R^d$, write $\langle u,z\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^d u_jz_j$ and $\|u\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d u_j^2)^{1/2}$, using the Euclidean convention in [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]].

For $\sigma^2\ge0$, a centered real random variable $X$ is **sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}\qquad\text{for every }\lambda\in\mathbb R.$$
A centered vector random element $Z\in\mathbb R^d$ is **sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda\langle u,Z\rangle}\le e^{\sigma^2\lambda^2\|u\|_2^2/2}\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathbb R^d\text{ and }\lambda\in\mathbb R.$$

For $\nu^2\ge0$ and $b>0$, a centered real random variable $X$ is **sub-exponential with parameters $(\nu^2,b)$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{\lambda^2\nu^2/2}\qquad\text{whenever }|\lambda|\le1/b.$$

The parameters $\sigma^2$ and $\nu^2$ are moment-generating-function upper-bound proxies; they are not asserted to equal the variance. The vector condition controls every one-dimensional projection and does not assert independence of coordinates.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid Borel $H$-valued random elements with $E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$. Let $\mu=E_BX_1$ be their Bochner mean, define $x\otimes y:h\mapsto\langle h,y\rangle x$, and let
$$
\Sigma=E_B[(X_1-\mu)\otimes(X_1-\mu)]\in S_1(H),\qquad V=\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=E\|X_1-\mu\|^2,
$$
where $E_B$ denotes Bochner expectation, $S_1(H)$ is the Banach space of trace-class operators on $H$, and $x\otimes y$ is the rank-one operator $h\mapsto\langle h,y\rangle x$.
For $0<p<a<1/2$, put $\psi(a;p)=a\log(a/p)+(1-a)\log((1-a)/(1-p))$ and $C_a=(1-a)/\sqrt{1-2a}$. Set $a=7/18$, $p=1/10$, and
$$
k=\left\lfloor\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{\psi(a;p)}\right\rfloor+1.
$$
If $0<\delta<1$ and $k\le n/2$, apply [[alg-geometric-median-of-block-means]] to $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ using $k$ blocks and call the output $\widehat\mu$. Then
$$
\mathbb P\!\left(\|\widehat\mu-\mu\|>11\sqrt{\frac{V\log(1.4/\delta)}{n}}\right)\le\delta.
$$
If $V>0$, the same bound holds with $\ge$ in place of $>$ in the displayed event. If $V=0$, then $\widehat\mu=\mu$ almost surely. The finite-variance assumption is on the clean iid sample; no sample-replacement or Huber-contamination guarantee is asserted here.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

The relation of [[def-real-order]] is well defined and makes $\mathbb{R}$
([[thm-reals-field]]) a totally ordered field.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

Every Cauchy sequence of real numbers ([[def-real-limit]]) converges to a real
number. Together with [[thm-reals-ordered-field]], this completes the
construction: $\mathbb{R}$ is a complete totally ordered field.
The proof uses no form of the axiom of choice.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

For a statistical experiment $\{P_\theta\}$ from [[def-statistical-experiment]], sample size $N\ge1$, and replacement fraction $0\le\eta\le1$, equip $\mathcal X^N$ with its finite product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). A sample-replacement coupling is a pair of $\mathcal X^N$-valued random elements on a common probability space ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]) $(X,Y)$ such that $X_1,\ldots,X_N$ are iid with law $P_\theta$ under [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]] and
$$
\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf1\{X_i\ne Y_i\}\le\lfloor\eta N\rfloor
$$
almost surely. Assume the diagonal $\Delta_{\mathcal X}=\{(x,x):x\in\mathcal X\}$ belongs to the product sigma-algebra $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A$ ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]), so each mismatch indicator is measurable. The joint law may depend on the entire clean sample; the observed vector $Y$ need not be iid.

Given a statistical experiment $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and any probability measure $Q$ on that space ([[def-probability-measure]]), Huber's one-observation contamination law is
$$
P_{\epsilon,\theta,Q}=(1-\epsilon)P_\theta+\epsilon Q,\qquad 0\le\epsilon\le1.
$$
The mixture is a probability measure by [[lem-convex-mixture-of-probability-laws]]. In the sample-size-$n$ model, observations are iid from this law ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]). A worst-case $Q$ may be chosen separately for each $\theta$. This is an iid sampling model, distinct from a fixed gross-error direction and from sample replacement.

derivations.claim: Under $P_0$, the clean sample of size $2N$ is all zero. Replace $N$ coordinates by $M$ to obtain the observed vector $(0,\ldots,0,M,\ldots,M)$ with $N$ entries of each value. This uses at most $\lfloor2\eta N\rfloor$ replacements by [F1].

Under $P_M$, the clean sample is all $M$. Replacing $N$ coordinates by $0$ produces exactly the same observed vector and also uses at most $\lfloor2\eta N\rfloor$ replacements. Both clean laws have variance zero, while their means are $0$ and $M$.

The two deterministic replacement couplings put probability one on the same observed vector. Hence the same Borel map $T$ has the same output value in both experiments. Exact recovery would require that value to equal $0$ under the first coupling and $M$ under the second, which is impossible because $M>0$. Both clean variances are zero, so any bound depending only on covariance and forcing zero error there would fail uniformly at $\eta\ge1/2$. The Huber mixture model in [F2] is not being used in this construction.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Every at most countable subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-countable]]) is Lebesgue measurable with

$$\lambda_n(E) \;=\; 0,$$

so $E$ is a $\lambda_n$-null set ([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).
In particular every singleton is null, and on the real line the set
$\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ of rational reals ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]) satisfies
$\lambda_1(\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}) = 0$.

Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on the same measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$. We say that $
u$ is **absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$**, and write
$$
u\ll\mu,$$
if every measurable $\mu$-null set is also $
u$-null:
$$\mu(E)=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
u(E)=0\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
Because every measurable subset of a $\mu$-null set is again $\mu$-null, this is equivalent to requiring $
u(F)=0$ for every measurable $F\subseteq E$ whenever $\mu(E)=0$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Every at most countable subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-countable]]) is Lebesgue measurable with

$$\lambda_n(E) \;=\; 0,$$

so $E$ is a $\lambda_n$-null set ([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).
In particular every singleton is null, and on the real line the set
$\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ of rational reals ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]) satisfies
$\lambda_1(\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}) = 0$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

The Cauchy-sequence reals $\mathbb{R}_C$ have the **least-upper-bound property**:
every nonempty $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_C$ that is bounded above has a least upper
bound $\sup S \in \mathbb{R}_C$. Hence, together with [[thm-reals-ordered-field]],
$\mathbb{R}_C$ is a **complete ordered field** ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

derivations.claim: For each $t\in\mathbb R$, the event $\{Z=t\}$ is measurable and its singleton is Lebesgue null by [F2]. Absolute continuity [F1] gives $P(Z=t)=0$. Therefore, if $t_n\uparrow t$, the events $\{Z\ge t_n\}$ decrease to $\{Z\ge t\}$ and [F3] gives $P(Z\ge t_n)\downarrow P(Z\ge t)$. If $t_n\downarrow t$ with $t_n>t$, these events increase to $\{Z>t\}$, so [F3] gives convergence to $P(Z>t)=P(Z\ge t)$. Thus the nonincreasing tail function $S(t)=P(Z\ge t)$ is continuous at every $t$.

As $n\to\infty$, the events $\{Z\ge n\}$ decrease to the empty set and $\{Z\ge -n\}$ increase to the whole sample space. By [F3], $S(n)\to0$ and $S(-n)\to1$. Since $1-u\in(0,1)$, the set $A=\{t:S(t)\ge1-u\}$ is nonempty and bounded above; [F4] gives its finite supremum. Continuity of $S$ makes $A$ closed, so that supremum $Q_u(Z)$ belongs to $A$.

If $S(Q_u(Z))>1-u$, continuity at $Q_u(Z)$ would give some $t>Q_u(Z)$ with $S(t)>1-u$, contradicting that $Q_u(Z)$ is an upper bound for $A$. Hence $S(Q_u(Z))=1-u$. Step 1.1 gives $P(Z=Q_u(Z))=0$, so $P(Z>Q_u(Z))=P(Z\ge Q_u(Z))=1-u$.

citations.quote:
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space, let
$T:V\to V$ be linear, and let $\mathcal E$ be an orthonormal basis of $V$. Write

$$A=[T]_{\mathcal E}^{\mathcal E}.$$

Then:

1. $T$ is self-adjoint if and only if $A=A^*$.
2. $T$ is normal if and only if $AA^*=A^*A$.

Over $\mathbb R$, $A^*$ is just $A^{\mathsf T}$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space, let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint, and let $v\in V$ be nonzero. The **Rayleigh quotient** of $v$ for
$T$ is

$$R_T(v):=\frac{\langle Tv,v\rangle}{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Because $\langle v,v\rangle>0$ for nonzero $v$ in an inner product space, this
quotient is a well-defined real number.

If $T$ is self-adjoint on a nonzero finite-dimensional real inner product space and its
eigenvalues are ordered as

$$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n,$$

then

$$\lambda_1=\max_{v\ne0} R_T(v)\qquad\text{and}\qquad \lambda_n=\min_{v\ne0} R_T(v).$$

derivations.claim: Each coordinate $X_r$ is square-integrable because $|X_r|\le\|X\|_2$, and is integrable since $|X_r|\le1+X_r^2$. Hence each $\mu_r$ is finite. Also $E[Y_r^2]\le2E[X_r^2]+2\mu_r^2<\infty$. For every $r,s$, the pointwise inequality $2|Y_rY_s|\le Y_r^2+Y_s^2$ gives $E|Y_rY_s|<\infty$, so every entry of $\Sigma$ exists. Since $Y_rY_s=Y_sY_r$, $\Sigma$ is symmetric.

For $v\in\mathbb R^d$, linearity of expectation [F2] and the finite-sum definition [F3] give $v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v=E[\langle v,Y\rangle^2]\ge0$, so $\Sigma$ is positive semidefinite. Summing its diagonal entries and using linearity again yields $\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=E[\sum_{r=1}^dY_r^2]=E\|Y\|_2^2$.

For nonzero $v$, [F5] identifies $\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)$ with the maximum Rayleigh quotient; pointwise Euclidean Cauchy–Schwarz gives $R_\Sigma(v)=E[\langle v,Y\rangle^2]/\|v\|_2^2\le E\|Y\|_2^2=\operatorname{tr}\Sigma$. Positive semidefiniteness from step 2.1 also gives $R_\Sigma(v)\ge0$, so maximizing proves $0\le\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\le\operatorname{tr}\Sigma$.

If $\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=0$, step 2.1 gives $E\|Y\|_2^2=0$. By [F1], the continuous polynomial $x\mapsto\|x-\mu\|_2^2$ composed with the Borel map $X$ is measurable, so [F4] applies and gives $\|Y\|_2^2=0$ almost surely. The Euclidean norm is positive definite, hence $Y=0$ almost surely and $X=\mu$ almost surely.

2. $T$ is normal if and only if $AA^*=A^*A$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space, let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint, and let $v\in V$ be nonzero. The **Rayleigh quotient** of $v$ for
$T$ is

$$R_T(v):=\frac{\langle Tv,v\rangle}{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Because $\langle v,v\rangle>0$ for nonzero $v$ in an inner product space, this
quotient is a well-defined real number.

If $T$ is self-adjoint on a nonzero finite-dimensional real inner product space and its

$$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n,$$

then

$$\lambda_1=\max_{v\ne0} R_T(v)\qquad\text{and}\qquad \lambda_n=\min_{v\ne0} R_T(v).$$

Let $N\ge1$ be an integer, let $\eta\ge0$, $0<\delta<1$, and set
$$
\varepsilon=8\eta+\frac{12\log(4/\delta)}{N}.
$$
The procedure is admissible when $0<\varepsilon\le1/4$. Its input is two observed real samples $\widetilde X_1,\ldots,\widetilde X_N$ and $\widetilde Y_1,\ldots,\widetilde Y_N$. Sort the second sample nondecreasingly as $\widetilde Y^*_{(1)}\le\cdots\le\widetilde Y^*_{(N)}$ and define $r(u)=\lceil uN\rceil$ for $0<u\le1$. Set
$$
\alpha=\widetilde Y^*_{(r(\varepsilon))},\qquad \beta=\widetilde Y^*_{(r(1-\varepsilon))},
$$
and, for $\alpha\le\beta$, let $\phi_{\alpha,\beta}(x)=\min\{\beta,\max\{\alpha,x\}\}$. Return
$$
\widehat\mu=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\phi_{\alpha,\beta}(\widetilde X_i).
$$
The operation is defined for every admissible input, including tied observations.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

derivations.claim: Since $0<\varepsilon\le1/4$, both $\varepsilon$ and $1-\varepsilon$ lie in $(0,1]$. Thus $1\le r(\varepsilon),r(1-\varepsilon)\le N$, and monotonicity of the ceiling gives $r(\varepsilon)\le r(1-\varepsilon)$. The corresponding sorted values therefore satisfy $\alpha\le\beta$, so every clipped value in [F1] is a finite real and the output is defined for every input, including ties.

For a scalar list $y_1,\ldots,y_N$, its $k$th order statistic equals $\min_{J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\},\,|J|=k}\max_{j\in J}y_j$: every $k$-subset has a maximum at least the $k$th smallest value, while the indices of the first $k$ sorted values attain it. This is a finite minimum of finite maxima of coordinate functions, hence is continuous in the list. The two cutoff maps in [F1] are therefore continuous; $\phi_{\alpha,\beta}(x)$ is continuous in $(\alpha,\beta,x)$ because it is a composition of minimum and maximum, and the final finite average is continuous. Hence the estimator is a continuous map on $\mathbb R^{2N}$.

For any Borel target set, its preimage under a continuous map is Borel: preimages of open sets are open, and the sets whose preimages are Borel form a sigma-algebra containing all open sets. By [F2] this is exactly Borel measurability, so the total estimator from step 1.1 is Borel.
