Let $d\ge1$ and let $X$ be a Borel random vector in $\mathbb R^d$ with $E\|X\|_2^2<\infty$. Define $\mu=EX$ coordinatewise, $Y=X-\mu$, and the finite matrix $\Sigma$ by $\Sigma_{rs}=E[Y_rY_s]$ for $1\le r,s\le d$. Then $\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite,
$$
\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=E\|X-\mu\|_2^2,
$$
and $0\le\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\le\operatorname{tr}\Sigma$. If $\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=0$, then $X=\mu$ almost surely.

For a statistical experiment $\{P_\theta\}$ from [[def-statistical-experiment]], sample size $N\ge1$, and replacement fraction $0\le\eta\le1$, equip $\mathcal X^N$ with its finite product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). A sample-replacement coupling is a pair of $\mathcal X^N$-valued random elements on a common probability space ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]) $(X,Y)$ such that $X_1,\ldots,X_N$ are iid with law $P_\theta$ under [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]] and
$$
\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf1\{X_i\ne Y_i\}\le\lfloor\eta N\rfloor
$$
almost surely. Assume the diagonal $\Delta_{\mathcal X}=\{(x,x):x\in\mathcal X\}$ belongs to the product sigma-algebra $\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A$ ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]), so each mismatch indicator is measurable. The joint law may depend on the entire clean sample; the observed vector $Y$ need not be iid.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $d,N\ge1$ be integers, let $0\le\eta\le1/10$, and let $0<\delta<1$ satisfy $N\ge2560\log(2/\delta)$. Given two observed halves $\widetilde X_1,\ldots,\widetilde X_N$ and $\widetilde Y_1,\ldots,\widetilde Y_N$ in $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$
\varepsilon=\max\left\{10\eta,\frac{2560\log(2/\delta)}{N}\right\}\in(0,1].
$$
For $v\in S^{d-1}$, sort $\langle\widetilde Y_i,v\rangle$ nondecreasingly and let $\alpha_v$ and $\beta_v$ be its order statistics of ranks $\lceil\varepsilon N/2\rceil$ and $\lceil(1-\varepsilon/2)N\rceil$. Write $\phi_{a,b}(t)=\min\{b,\max\{a,t\}\}$. For $Q>0$ define
$$U_Q(v)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\phi_{\alpha_v-Q,\,\beta_v+Q}(\langle\widetilde X_i,v\rangle),\qquad \Gamma(v,Q)=\{z\in\mathbb R^d:|\langle z,v\rangle-U_Q(v)|\le2\varepsilon Q\}.$$
and $\Gamma(Q)=\bigcap_{v\in S^{d-1}}\Gamma(v,Q)$. For each $j\in\mathbb Z$, put
$$
K_j=\bigcap_{i\ge j}\Gamma(2^i),\qquad S=\{j\in\mathbb Z:K_j\ne\varnothing\}.
$$
Return the unique minimum-norm point of $K_j$ if $S$ has least element $j$; if $S=\mathbb Z$, return the unique minimum-norm point of $\bigcap_{i\in\mathbb Z}\Gamma(2^i)$; if $S=\varnothing$, return the first-half sample mean $N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\widetilde X_i$. This three-branch selector is total on the displayed input domain; its existence and Borel measurability are proved in [[lem-multivariate-trimmed-mean-selector-total-and-measurable]].

and $\Gamma(Q)=\bigcap_{v\in S^{d-1}}\Gamma(v,Q)$. For each $j\in\mathbb Z$, put
$$

Return the unique minimum-norm point of $K_j$ if $S$ has least element $j$; if $S=\mathbb Z$, return the unique minimum-norm point of $\bigcap_{i\in\mathbb Z}\Gamma(2^i)$; if $S=\varnothing$, return the first-half sample mean $N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\widetilde X_i$. This three-branch selector is total on the displayed input domain; its existence and Borel measurability are proved in [[lem-multivariate-trimmed-mean-selector-total-and-measurable]].

For each fixed admissible $d,N,\varepsilon$ and each observed data tuple in $(\mathbb R^d)^{2N}$, the procedure [[alg-multivariate-trimmed-mean]] returns a unique vector in $\mathbb R^d$. The fallback branch covers the case where no dyadic tail intersection is nonempty; the all-scale branch covers the case where every tail intersection is nonempty.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and iid sampling in [F2], with probability one every clean coordinate in both halves equals $\mu$. Fix any such clean realization and any admissible replacement output. Each observed half has at most $m\le\lfloor2\eta N\rfloor\le2\eta N\le\varepsilon N/5$ changed coordinates. Put $q=\varepsilon N/2$, so $m<q\le N/2$. The two ranks in [F3] are $r_- =\lceil q\rceil$ and $r_+=\lceil N-q\rceil=N-\lfloor q\rfloor$. They satisfy $m<r_-,r_+$ and $r_-,r_+\le N-m$: indeed $r_-\le\lceil N/2\rceil\le N-m$, while $r_+\ge\lceil N/2\rceil>m$ and $r_+=N-\lfloor q\rfloor\le N-m$. Thus for every unit $v$, both order statistics of the second half equal $\langle\mu,v\rangle$, since the unaltered projections occupy all ranks from $m+1$ through $N-m$.

For any $Q>0$ and unit $v$, the unaltered first-half projections equal $\langle\mu,v\rangle$, while each changed projection after clipping to $[\langle\mu,v\rangle-Q,\langle\mu,v\rangle+Q]$ differs from it by at most $Q$. By step 1.1 these are the clipping endpoints used by [F3], so $|U_Q(v)-\langle\mu,v\rangle|\le mQ/N\le2\eta Q\le\varepsilon Q/5<2\varepsilon Q$. Hence $\mu\in\Gamma(Q)$ for every dyadic $Q=2^i$, and $\mu\in K_j$ for every integer $j$. Therefore $S=\mathbb Z$ in [F3].

Let $z$ belong to the algorithm's all-scale intersection. For each fixed unit $v$ and every integer $i$, its slab constraint and step 2.1 imply $|\langle z-\mu,v\rangle|\le|\langle z,v\rangle-U_{2^i}(v)|+|U_{2^i}(v)-\langle\mu,v\rangle|\le2\varepsilon2^i+2\eta2^i$. Letting $i\to-\infty$ gives $\langle z-\mu,v\rangle=0$ for every unit $v$. If $z\ne\mu$, choosing $v=(z-\mu)/\|z-\mu\|_2$ contradicts that equality; thus the all-scale intersection is exactly $\{\mu\}$. Since $S=\mathbb Z$, [F3] and [F5] make the algorithm return its unique point $\mu$. The argument holds on the probability-one event from step 1.1, proving the claim.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $Z$ be a real random variable whose law is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$. For $0<u<1$, define
$$
Q_u(Z)=\sup\{t\in\mathbb R:P(Z\ge t)\ge1-u\}.
$$
Then $Q_u(Z)$ is finite and
$$
P(Z\ge Q_u(Z))=P(Z>Q_u(Z))=1-u.
$$

Let $Z$ be a real random variable whose law is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$. For $0<u<1$, define
$$
Q_u(Z)=\sup\{t\in\mathbb R:P(Z\ge t)\ge1-u\}.
$$
Then $Q_u(Z)$ is finite and
$$
P(Z\ge Q_u(Z))=P(Z>Q_u(Z))=1-u.
$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

For $p\in[0,1]$, a **Bernoulli$(p)$ random variable** takes the value $1$ with probability $p$ and $0$ with probability $1-p$.

For $n\in\mathbb N$, a **binomial$(n,p)$ random variable** is a sum $X=\sum_{i<n}X_i$ of $n$ mutually independent Bernoulli$(p)$ variables. When $n=0$, this is the constant zero random variable.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

derivations.claim: Put $\eta=0$ and $\delta=4e^{-N/120}$. For sufficiently large $N$, $0<\delta<1$ and $\delta\ge e^{-N/4}$ because $4e^{29N/120}>1$. The theorem's definition then gives $\varepsilon=8\eta+12\log(4/\delta)/N=1/10$. Hence $p=\varepsilon/2=1/20$, $q=3\varepsilon/4=3/40$, and the asserted failure exponent is $\varepsilon/12=1/120$.

By [F1], each indicator $\mathbf1\{Z_i>Q_{19/20}(Z)\}$ has success probability $1/20$; iid sampling and [F2] give $B_N\sim\operatorname{Bin}(N,p)$ with $p=1/20$. At $q=3/40$, its relative-entropy rate is $D(q\|p)=q\log(q/p)+(1-q)\log((1-q)/(1-p))=\frac3{40}\log\frac32+\frac{37}{40}\log\frac{37}{38}$.

Let $m=qN+1$, an integer because $40\mid N$. For $p_m=m/N$, the binomial point-mass ratio $\mathbb P_{p_m}(B_N=j+1)/\mathbb P_{p_m}(B_N=j)=((N-j)/(j+1))(p_m/(1-p_m))$ is greater than $1$ at $j=m-1$ and less than $1$ at $j=m$, and decreases with $j$. Thus $m$ is a mode of $\operatorname{Bin}(N,p_m)$, whose $N+1$ masses sum to one; consequently $\mathbb P_{p_m}(B_N=m)\ge1/(N+1)$. The binomial formula and [F4] give $\mathbb P_p(B_N=m)=\mathbb P_{p_m}(B_N=m)e^{-ND(p_m\|p)}\ge e^{-ND(p_m\|p)}/(N+1)$. By continuity of $D(r\|p)$ in $r$, [F4] and step 3.1 give $D(p_m\|p)\to D(q\|p)<1/120$. Choose $c>0$ with $D(q\|p)+c<1/120$. For all sufficiently large such $N$, $D(p_m\|p)<1/120-c$ and [F5] gives $e^{cN}\ge1+cN+(cN)^2/2>N+1$. Therefore $\mathbb P_p(B_N=m)>e^{-N/120}$. Since $m>3N/40$, this mass lies in $\{B_N>3N/40\}$, disproving the displayed source bound at the admissible parameters from step 1.1.

Let $Z$ be a real random variable whose law is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$. For $0<u<1$, define
$$
Q_u(Z)=\sup\{t\in\mathbb R:P(Z\ge t)\ge1-u\}.
$$
Then $Q_u(Z)$ is finite and
$$
P(Z\ge Q_u(Z))=P(Z>Q_u(Z))=1-u.
$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

For $p\in[0,1]$, a **Bernoulli$(p)$ random variable** takes the value $1$ with probability $p$ and $0$ with probability $1-p$.

For $n\in\mathbb N$, a **binomial$(n,p)$ random variable** is a sum $X=\sum_{i<n}X_i$ of $n$ mutually independent Bernoulli$(p)$ variables. When $n=0$, this is the constant zero random variable.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

Let $d,N\ge1$ be integers, let $0\le\eta\le1/10$, and let $0<\delta<1$ satisfy $N\ge2560\log(2/\delta)$. Given two observed halves $\widetilde X_1,\ldots,\widetilde X_N$ and $\widetilde Y_1,\ldots,\widetilde Y_N$ in $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$
\varepsilon=\max\left\{10\eta,\frac{2560\log(2/\delta)}{N}\right\}\in(0,1].
$$
For $v\in S^{d-1}$, sort $\langle\widetilde Y_i,v\rangle$ nondecreasingly and let $\alpha_v$ and $\beta_v$ be its order statistics of ranks $\lceil\varepsilon N/2\rceil$ and $\lceil(1-\varepsilon/2)N\rceil$. Write $\phi_{a,b}(t)=\min\{b,\max\{a,t\}\}$. For $Q>0$ define
$$U_Q(v)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\phi_{\alpha_v-Q,\,\beta_v+Q}(\langle\widetilde X_i,v\rangle),\qquad \Gamma(v,Q)=\{z\in\mathbb R^d:|\langle z,v\rangle-U_Q(v)|\le2\varepsilon Q\}.$$
and $\Gamma(Q)=\bigcap_{v\in S^{d-1}}\Gamma(v,Q)$. For each $j\in\mathbb Z$, put
$$
K_j=\bigcap_{i\ge j}\Gamma(2^i),\qquad S=\{j\in\mathbb Z:K_j\ne\varnothing\}.
$$
Return the unique minimum-norm point of $K_j$ if $S$ has least element $j$; if $S=\mathbb Z$, return the unique minimum-norm point of $\bigcap_{i\in\mathbb Z}\Gamma(2^i)$; if $S=\varnothing$, return the first-half sample mean $N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\widetilde X_i$. This three-branch selector is total on the displayed input domain; its existence and Borel measurability are proved in [[lem-multivariate-trimmed-mean-selector-total-and-measurable]].

For each fixed admissible $d,N,\varepsilon$ and each observed data tuple in $(\mathbb R^d)^{2N}$, the procedure [[alg-multivariate-trimmed-mean]] returns a unique vector in $\mathbb R^d$. As a function of the observed data tuple it is Borel measurable. The fallback branch covers the case where no dyadic tail intersection is nonempty; the all-scale branch covers the case where every tail intersection is nonempty.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $X$ be a Borel random vector in $\mathbb R^d$ with $E\|X\|_2^2<\infty$. Define $\mu=EX$ coordinatewise, $Y=X-\mu$, and the finite matrix $\Sigma$ by $\Sigma_{rs}=E[Y_rY_s]$ for $1\le r,s\le d$. Then $\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite,
$$
\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=E\|X-\mu\|_2^2,
$$
and $0\le\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\le\operatorname{tr}\Sigma$. If $\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=0$, then $X=\mu$ almost surely.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim: Since $K_{i_0}\ne\varnothing$, $i_0\in S$. If $S=\mathbb Z$, [F1] puts the algorithm output in $\bigcap_{i\in\mathbb Z}\Gamma(2^i)\subseteq K_{i_0}$. If $S$ is nonempty and proper, its least element $j_*$ satisfies $j_*\le i_0$, so nesting in [F1] gives $K_{j_*}\subseteq K_{i_0}$ and the output again belongs to $K_{i_0}$. Thus the event condition implies $\|\widehat\mu-\mu\|_2\le b\varepsilon Q_0$.

The definition of $Q_0$ gives $b\varepsilon Q_0\le256b\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}\Sigma/N}+16b\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\varepsilon}$. Since $\varepsilon\le10\eta+2560\log(2/\delta)/N$, square-root subadditivity and [F3] bound the second term by $16b\sqrt{10\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\eta}+16b\sqrt{2560\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\log(1/\delta)/N}+16b\sqrt{2560\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\log2/N}$. By [F2] the final term is at most $16b\sqrt{2560\log2}\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}\Sigma/N}$. These three coefficients are bounded by $c_b$, giving the stated implication. At $b=4$ this is exactly the previous constant.

Every complete ordered field $F$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) is Archimedean:
for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
([[def-ordered-field]]). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathbb{R}$ is the ambient ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-field]]).

**Natural exponents.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to
the set $\mathbb{R}$, the starting element $1$ and the function
$f(x) = x \cdot a$, there is a unique function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$,
written $n \mapsto a^n$, with

$$a^0 = 1, \qquad a^{n+1} = a^n \cdot a \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Thus $a^1 = a$, $a^2 = a \cdot a$, and so on. Note that this is defined for
**every** $a$, including $a = 0$.

**Negative exponents.** If $a \ne 0$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, set

$$a^{-n} := (a^n)^{-1}.$$

**Why that is legitimate.** The right-hand side presupposes that $a^n$ is
invertible, that is, that $a^n \ne 0$. This is a proof obligation and not an
observation, and it is discharged by claim 2 of [[lem-power-laws]]: for $a \ne 0$
in a field, $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, proved there by induction on
$n$ from the fact that a field has no zero divisors ([[lem-of-no-zero-divisors]]).
That lemma is a statement *about* the operation introduced here, so it depends on
this definition and is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its
`deps` (SCHEMA §3). Given $a^n \ne 0$, the value $(a^n)^{-1}$ is a single
well-determined element, because multiplicative inverses in a field are unique
([[lem-of-inverse-unique]]).

**Integer exponents.** Every integer $m$ ([[def-integers]]) is either
$n$ or $-n$ for a unique natural $n$, where $n$ in these integer expressions denotes its image under the
embedding $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]],
[[def-int-operations]]). This too is a citation and not a slogan: the order on
$\mathbb{Z}$ is total ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]), so $m \ge 0$ or $m < 0$; the
image of $\iota$ is exactly the set of nonnegative integers, and each of them is
$n$ for a unique natural $n$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]); and if $m < 0$ then
$-m > 0$, by compatibility of the order with addition ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]),
so $-m = n$ and $m = -n$, with $n$ unique because $\iota$ is
injective. The two clauses above therefore define $a^m$ for every
$m \in \mathbb{Z}$ whenever $a \ne 0$, and for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$ for
arbitrary $a$. The two exponent domains are disjoint: the natural clause
handles $m \ge 0$, including $m = 0$, while the negative clause requires
$n \ge 1$ and therefore handles only $m < 0$.

Let $a, b$ be elements of a field ([[def-field]]) and let integer powers be as in
[[def-integer-power]].

1. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$: $a^{m+n} = a^m a^n$, $(a^m)^n = a^{mn}$ and $(ab)^n = a^n b^n$.
2. If $a \ne 0$ then $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and $a^{-m} = (a^m)^{-1}$ for every $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ ([[def-int-operations]]).
3. If $a \ne 0$ and $b \ne 0$ then all three identities of claim 1 hold for all $m, n \in \mathbb{Z}$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], choose an integer $n\ge1$ with $n+1>\max\{a,1/a\}$. By induction from [F2], $2^n\ge n+1>a$, while $2^{-n}=1/2^n\le1/(n+1)<a$.

In the finite ordered list of integers $-n,-n+1,\ldots,n$, take the least $i$ with $2^i\ge a$; it exists because exponent $n$ qualifies and exponent $-n$ does not. Thus $i>-n$, so $i-1$ is in the list and fails the defining inequality: $2^{i-1}<a\le2^i$. The power law in [F2] gives $2^i=2\cdot2^{i-1}<2a$.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $X$ be an
integrable real random variable, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval
containing $X(\omega)$ for almost every $\omega$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$
be convex.

Assume additionally that $\varphi(X)$ is either integrable or nonnegative, so
its expectation is defined by
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Then
$$\varphi(\mathbb E[X])\le\mathbb E[\varphi(X)].$$
In the nonnegative case the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

derivations.claim: For positive bounded $U$ bounded away from zero, define $\operatorname{Ent}(U)=E[U\log U]-EU\log EU$. The function $\Phi(u,a)=u\log(u/a)-u+a$ is jointly convex: its Hessian quadratic form is $(du-(u/a)da)^2/u\ge0$. Direct differentiation in $a$ gives $\operatorname{Ent}(U)=\inf_{a>0}E\Phi(U,a)$, attained at $a=EU$. If $E_i$ integrates coordinate $i$, the product identity $\operatorname{Ent}(U)=E_{-i}\operatorname{Ent}_i(U)+\operatorname{Ent}_{-i}(E_iU)$ is obtained by adding and subtracting $E[(E_iU)\log(E_iU)]$. Joint convexity gives $\operatorname{Ent}_j(E_iU)\le E_i\operatorname{Ent}_j(U)$ for $j\ne i$: apply Jensen to $\Phi(E_iU,E_iE_jU)$ and integrate coordinate $j$. Induction in the product identity proves tensorization $\operatorname{Ent}(U)\le E\sum_i\operatorname{Ent}_i(U)$. All integrations here are on finite product laws.

Let $Z_i'$ replace $X_i$ by an independent copy and put $V_+=\sum_i E_i'(Z-Z_i')_+^2$. Jensen for the logarithm gives $\operatorname{Ent}_i(e^{tZ})\le\operatorname{Cov}_i(e^{tZ},tZ)$ for $t>0$. A fresh-copy expansion expresses this covariance as $\frac t2E_{i,i'}[(e^{tZ}-e^{tZ_i'})(Z-Z_i')]$. Swap the two copies to restrict to $Z>Z_i'$ and use $1-e^{-ta}\le ta$ for $a\ge0$. Tensorization from step 1.1 then yields $\operatorname{Ent}(e^{tZ})\le t^2E[e^{tZ}V_+]$. Choose the first maximizing function $f_*$ for $Z$ in a fixed finite ordering. Since $Z-Z_i'\le f_*(X_i)-f_*(X_i')$, the bound $(a-b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2$ gives $V_+\le2W+2ns^2$.

Write $c=B^2$ and $W_i=\sup_f\sum_{j\ne i}f(X_j)^2$. Choosing a common maximizer for $W$ shows $0\le\Delta_i=W-W_i\le c$ and $\sum_i\Delta_i\le W$. Use the conditional variational formula of step 1.1 with comparator $e^{aW_i}$, which is independent of coordinate $i$. With $\psi(u)=e^u-u-1$, it gives $\operatorname{Ent}_i(e^{aW})\le E_i[e^{aW}\psi(-a\Delta_i)]$. Convexity and $\psi(0)=0$ imply $\psi(-a\Delta_i)\le(\Delta_i/c)\psi(-ac)$. Tensorization therefore implies, for $L(a)=\log Ee^{aW}$, $aL'(a)-L(a)\le\psi(-ac)L'(a)/c$, or $(1-e^{-ac})L'(a)\le cL(a)$. If $m=0$, $W=0$ almost surely and the following bound is immediate. Otherwise differentiating $L(a)/(e^{ac}-1)$ shows it is nonincreasing; its limit at zero is $m/c$. Thus $L(a)\le(m/c)(e^{ac}-1)\le2am$ whenever $0\le ac\le1/2$, where the last scalar inequality follows by integrating $e^u\le2$ on $[0,1/2]$.

Put $H(t)=\log Ee^{tZ}$ and $D=tH'(t)-H(t)$, and let $E_t$ denote integration against density $e^{tZ-H(t)}$. Step 2.1 gives $D\le2t^2E_tW+2t^2ns^2$. Jensen under this tilted law applied to $e^{aW}/e^{tZ-H(t)}$ gives $aE_tW\le L(a)+D$; indeed its expectation under the tilt is $Ee^{aW}$, while the expectation of its logarithm is $aE_tW-D$. Taking $a=4t^2$ and using step 2.2 yields $D\le(8m+4ns^2)t^2$ for $0<t\le1/(\sqrt8 B)$. Integrating $(H(t)/t)'=D/t^2$ from zero proves $\log Ee^{t(Z-EZ)}\le At^2$, where $A=8m+4ns^2$.

Put $b=\sqrt8 B$. If $A>0$, choose $t=\sqrt{x}/(\sqrt A+b\sqrt x)<1/b$. Markov's inequality and step 3.1 show that a deviation of size $At+x/t$ has probability at most $e^{-x}$. Since $At+x/t\le2\sqrt{Ax}+bx$, the stated tail bound follows. The case $A=0$ follows by taking $t\uparrow1/b$ in the same exponential bound. Finally enumerate a countable class with zero first and increase its finite initial subclasses. Let $d,N\ge1$ be integers, let $0\le\eta\le1/10$, and let $0<\delta<1$ satisfy $N\ge2560\log(2/\delta)$. Given two observed halves $\widetilde X_1,\ldots,\widetilde X_N$ and $\widetilde Y_1,\ldots,\widetilde Y_N$ in $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$
\varepsilon=\max\left\{10\eta,\frac{2560\log(2/\delta)}{N}\right\}\in(0,1].
$$
For $v\in S^{d-1}$, sort $\langle\widetilde Y_i,v\rangle$ nondecreasingly and let $\alpha_v$ and $\beta_v$ be its order statistics of ranks $\lceil\varepsilon N/2\rceil$ and $\lceil(1-\varepsilon/2)N\rceil$. Write $\phi_{a,b}(t)=\min\{b,\max\{a,t\}\}$. For $Q>0$ define
$$U_Q(v)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\phi_{\alpha_v-Q,\,\beta_v+Q}(\langle\widetilde X_i,v\rangle),\qquad \Gamma(v,Q)=\{z\in\mathbb R^d:|\langle z,v\rangle-U_Q(v)|\le2\varepsilon Q\}.$$
and $\Gamma(Q)=\bigcap_{v\in S^{d-1}}\Gamma(v,Q)$. For each $j\in\mathbb Z$, put
$$
K_j=\bigcap_{i\ge j}\Gamma(2^i),\qquad S=\{j\in\mathbb Z:K_j\ne\varnothing\}.
$$
Return the unique minimum-norm point of $K_j$ if $S$ has least element $j$; if $S=\mathbb Z$, return the unique minimum-norm point of $\bigcap_{i\in\mathbb Z}\Gamma(2^i)$; if $S=\varnothing$, return the first-half sample mean $N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\widetilde X_i$. This three-branch selector is total on the displayed input domain; its existence and Borel measurability are proved in [[lem-multivariate-trimmed-mean-selector-total-and-measurable]].

Let $d\ge1$ and let $X$ be a Borel random vector in $\mathbb R^d$ with $E\|X\|_2^2<\infty$. Define $\mu=EX$ coordinatewise, $Y=X-\mu$, and the finite matrix $\Sigma$ by $\Sigma_{rs}=E[Y_rY_s]$ for $1\le r,s\le d$. Then $\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite,
$$
\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=E\|X-\mu\|_2^2,
$$
and $0\le\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\le\operatorname{tr}\Sigma$. If $\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=0$, then $X=\mu$ almost surely.

The unique dyadic scale in $[2Q_0,4Q_0)$ is $Q=32$, so $i_0=5$. All parameters belong to the asserted domain, and zero actual replacements is allowed when the known upper fraction is $1/10$.

Every observed point and directional cutoff lies in $[-1,1]$. For every dyadic $R\ge32$, the expanded clipping interval contains $[-1,1]$ in each of the two unit directions. Thus $U_R(1)=\bar X$, $U_R(-1)=-\bar X$, and $\Gamma(R)=[\bar X-2R,\bar X+2R]$. These intervals are nested, so $K_5=[\bar X-64,\bar X+64]$. Let $N\ge1$ be an integer, let $\eta\ge0$, $0<\delta<1$, and set
$$
\varepsilon=8\eta+\frac{12\log(4/\delta)}{N}.
$$
The procedure is admissible when $0<\varepsilon\le1/4$. Its input is two observed real samples $\widetilde X_1,\ldots,\widetilde X_N$ and $\widetilde Y_1,\ldots,\widetilde Y_N$. Sort the second sample nondecreasingly as $\widetilde Y^*_{(1)}\le\cdots\le\widetilde Y^*_{(N)}$ and define $r(u)=\lceil uN\rceil$ for $0<u\le1$. Set
$$
\alpha=\widetilde Y^*_{(r(\varepsilon))},\qquad \beta=\widetilde Y^*_{(r(1-\varepsilon))},
$$
and, for $\alpha\le\beta$, let $\phi_{\alpha,\beta}(x)=\min\{\beta,\max\{\alpha,x\}\}$. Return
$$
\widehat\mu=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\phi_{\alpha,\beta}(\widetilde X_i).
$$
The operation is defined for every admissible input, including tied observations.

Let $Z$ be a real random variable whose law is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$. For $0<u<1$, define
$$
Q_u(Z)=\sup\{t\in\mathbb R:P(Z\ge t)\ge1-u\}.
$$
Then $Q_u(Z)$ is finite and
$$
P(Z\ge Q_u(Z))=P(Z>Q_u(Z))=1-u.
$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

If $X$ is a square-integrable real random variable and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(|X-\mathbb E[X]|\ge a)\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{a^2}.$$

derivations.claim: This law is absolutely continuous with density $1/(4w)$ on each interval $[-1-w,-1+w]$ and $[1-w,1+w]$, has mean zero and variance $\sigma^2=1+w^2/3$. The replacement rule is a measurable finite-coordinate rule and makes at most $20000=2\eta N$ changes. Put $\varepsilon=.08+12\log40/10^6$, so $.08<\varepsilon<.081<1/4$, and $\delta\ge e^{-N/4}$. At lower tail mass $2\varepsilon$ the quantile is $-1-w+8w\varepsilon$. Integration over the lower interval gives $E[(Q_{2\varepsilon}-X)\mathbf1_{\{X\le Q_{2\varepsilon}\}}]=(8w\varepsilon)^2/(8w)=8w\varepsilon^2$; symmetry gives the same upper-tail excess. Hence $3E_{\mathrm{exc}}(4\varepsilon)+2\sigma\sqrt{\log40/10^6}<.0042$, using $\log40<4$, $\varepsilon<.081$ and $\sigma^2<1.000001$.

Let $A$ be the event that the clean first-half sign average has absolute value at most $.01$, and let $B$ be the event that the second-half negative-sign count lies between $N/4$ and $3N/4$. The sign average has variance $1/N$, so [F3] gives $P(A^c)\le.01$. The second-half count has variance $N/4$, so $P(B^c)\le4/N$. On $A$ there are at least $.495N$ negative first-half signs, so the replacement changes exactly $20000$ of them. The resulting sign average is at least $-.01+.04=.03$. On $B$, the ranks in [F1] put $\alpha$ in the negative interval and $\beta$ in the positive interval, since $\varepsilon<.081<1/4$. Every clipped value is at least its altered sign minus $w$: a negative value is at least $-1-w$, and a positive value, including a replacement $+1$, clips to at least $1-w$. Therefore $\widehat\mu\ge.03-w=.029$ on $A\cap B$, whose probability is at least $.989996$. This exceeds the proposed threshold $.0042$ with probability greater than $\delta=.1$, disproving the asserted coverage.
